articles.title: Acusado de matar homem com tábua de carne é condenado em SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Hunberto Agustinho da Silva foi preso em flagrante após matar Marcio Jose Boer, de 46 anos, dentro de casa, em Rio Claro (SP). Crime aconteceu em 8 de maio de 2025.
articles.summary: Hunberto Agustinho da Silva foi preso em flagrante após matar Marcio Jose Boer, de 46 anos, dentro de casa, em Rio Claro (SP). Crime aconteceu em 8 de maio de 2025.
articles.body:
Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM) de Rio Claro (SP) atendeu o caso de homicídio — Foto: Guarda Civil Municipal

Hunberto Agustinho da Silva foi condenado a 21 anos e 8 meses de prisão , em regime inicial fechado, por matar Marcio Jose Boer, de 46 anos, com golpes de tábua de cortar carnes em Rio Claro (SP). De acordo com a sentença de terça-feira (22), ele não poderá recorrer em liberdade.

O crime aconteceu na tarde de 8 de maio de 2025 em uma casa localizada na Rua 12, no bairro Santa Cruz. Hunberto foi preso em flagrante pela Guarda Civil Municipal (GCM).

O g1 não localizou a defesa de Hunberto até a última atualização desta reportagem.

De acordo com o Ministério Público do Estado de São Paulo (MP-SP), a sentença atestou a prática de fraude processual, assim como a presença das qualificadoras de motivo torpe, meio cruel e recurso que impossibilitou a defesa da vítima.

Conforme a denúncia oferecida pela promotora de Justiça Maria Claudia Cruz de Oliveira, o crime ocorreu dentro da residência onde a vítima e o réu moravam e costumavam usar drogas.

Após uma discussão, Hunberto determinou que Marcio deixasse o imóvel e o ameaçou de morte. Diante da recusa, apoderou-se de uma tábua de madeira utilizada para cortar alimentos e desferiu diversos golpes contra a cabeça, o pescoço, o tórax e os membros da vítima.

De acordo com o MP-SP, mesmo após Marcio estar gravemente ferido e incapacitado, o réu ateou fogo em parte do corpo dele, provocando queimaduras enquanto a vítima ainda apresentava sinais de vida.

O homem sofreu múltiplas fraturas nas costelas, perfuração pulmonar e lesões no pescoço, que provocaram asfixia mecânica , de acordo com o laudo necroscópico. Também foram identificadas lesões de defesa nos braços e nas mãos, indicando que a vítima tentou resistir à agressão.

A promotoria afirmou que o réu tentou alterar a cena do crime , arrastando o corpo para outro cômodo, lavando o local e removendo vestígios de sangue. O julgamento foi realizado pelo Tribunal do Júri de Rio Claro, com atuação em plenário do promotor de Justiça Cássio Sartori.n

Ao justificar a qualificadora do motivo torpe, a promotora Maria Claudia apontou que a conduta criminosa revelou "absoluto desprezo pela vida humana".

Segundo informações do Boletim de Ocorrência, a GCM foi chamada e, ao chegar ao local, encontrou a vítima sem vida em um quadro com diversas lesões pelo corpo aparentemente provocadas por instrumento contundente e outras com aparência de queimaduras. O Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) constatou o óbito.

Os GCMs encontraram Hunberto lavando a cozinha e limpando portas e o quintal, pois estavam com manchas de sangue .

Segundo os guardas, o Hunberto contou que vivia com a vítima há aproximadamente um mês na casa e que sempre consumiam drogas. Ele disse ainda que não sabia o motivo da morte de Marcio e que foi ele quem solicitou a um vizinho para chamar o socorro.

De acordo com o B.O., depois que os socorristas do Samu deixaram o local, Hunmberto voltou atrás a contou aos GCMs o que realmente aconteceu.

Segundo ele, Marcio consumiu drogas, possivelmente cocaína ou crack, e ficou muito alterado. Em meio a uma discussão, ele teria pedido para que Marcio saísse da casa, pois caso contrário iria matá-lo.

Caso foi registrado no Plantão Policial de Rio Claro — Foto: Gabriela Ferraz/EPTV

Como Marcio não o atendeu, Hunberto afirmou que pegou uma tábua de madeira utilizada para cortar alimentos na cozinha e desferiu alguns golpes na cabeça e corpo com a vontade de matá-lo. A vítima ficou cambaleante e passou a perder sangue, tendo chegado a entrar em um banheiro do lado externo do imóvel, e logo em seguida caiu na cozinha, já sem vida.

Hunberto disse ainda aos GCMs que, enquanto o Samu não chegava, ele arrastou o corpo de Marcio até a cama em que ele foi encontrado sem vida e passou a limpar as manchas de sangue, mas não deu tempo de completar a tarefa.

Os guardas civis preservaram o local para a Polícia Científica realizar o trabalho de perícia. A tábua utilizada no crime foi estava sobre a pia da cozinha e nela havia manchas de sangue.

Ainda segundo o boletim a irmã da vítima compareceu ao local e disse que Marcio havia recebido a casa como herança. De acordo com a irmã, ele era usuário de drogas e ela não sabia que o irmão havia deixado outras pessoas morar no imóvel , já que ela não visitava Marcio há aproximadamente quatro meses. Ela não conhecia Hunberto.

Preso em flagrante, o agressor foi levado para a Unidade de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) do bairro do Estádio e depois encaminhado para o Plantão Policial. Ele não respondeu nenhuma pergunta, afirmou que só iria falar somente na Justiça e que não iria assinar nenhum documento.

Hunberto foi encaminhado ao Setor Carcerário da Delegacia Seccional de Polícia de Rio Claro. Já o corpo de Marcio foi levado para o Instituto Médico Legal (IML) de Rio Claro.

articles.title: 'When they ask why you are unhappy, I…’: Behind Vaikom Vijayalakshmi’s National Award is a journey through blindness, insensitive questions and choosing freedom on her own terms
articles.summary: Voices of Power News: When Vaikom Vijayalakshmi walked up to receive the National Award for Best Female Playback Singer, the moment marked recognition for a voice that mill.
articles.body: When Vaikom Vijayalakshmi walked up to receive the National Award for Best Female Playback Singer, the moment marked recognition for a voice that millions have heard. But behind that voice is a woman who has spent much of her life negotiating something far more personal: how the world sees a person who cannot see it.Vijayalakshmi received the National Award for Best Female Playback Singer for “Angu Vaana Konilu” from Ajayante Randam Moshanam at the 72nd National Film Awards. The recognition came years after she entered the playback singing industry, but the award is only one part of a journey that has included professional success, repeated attempts to find a treatment for her blindness, insensitive encounters with strangers and a marriage she eventually chose to leave.Speaking to TOI after the national award was announced, Vijayalakshmi said the song’s words had particular meaning for her. “The lyrics ‘Uyarnnu Vaa... Uyarnnu Vaa... Break every barrier and rise... Conquer the world and rise...’ always fill me with the strength to move forward. I, too, have overcome countless obstacles to reach where I am today,” she said. Those obstacles have not always been visible to those around her.‘I get angry when people treat me differently because I am blind’Vijayalakshmi was born visually impaired and has lived with very limited perception of light. She has often spoken about how differently people behave around her once they realise she cannot see.In an interview with Cineulagam Tamil Channel, she described one particular behaviour that frustrates her: people trying to test whether she can recognise them by their voice.“I get angry when I see the way some people treat me as I am blind,” she said. She does not appreciate being asked questions such as whether she knows who someone is or being made to identify people by their voices.“I hate questions such as do you understand who I am, who hand is this and testing me like who the person is that by listening to their voice,” she said. “What is the use of recognizing people like that?”For her, the problem is not that she cannot answer. It is the assumption behind the question- that her blindness makes her someone who needs to be tested. “When they ask why you are unhappy, I will say I don't like to answer such questions,” she said.Vijayalakshmi has previously said that she can perceive only a little light and distinguish between night and day.Yet the absence of sight has not meant an absence of awareness. Much of Vijayalakshmi’s understanding of the world has been built through sound- something that eventually became the foundation of her career.Music became a way of experiencing the worldVijayalakshmi began singing when she was very young. Her parents, Muraleedharan and Vimala, supported her musical training and remained closely involved in her journey.She grew up listening to musicians such as K J Yesudas, M S Subbulakshmi, Balamuralikrishna and Chembai Swamikal. She eventually became a professional singer and went on to work in several Indian languages.But music, for Vijayalakshmi, is not simply a profession. It is also one of the ways through which she experiences things she cannot see.That is why ordinary moments involving sight can sometimes affect her deeply. “If someone buys something and doesn't show it to me I will feel sad. I feel like I am being ignored because I am blind,” she said.It is a small example, but it reveals something larger about what she has wanted from people around her: not special treatment, but inclusion. Her parents have remained an important part of that support system.“Father and mother will be always there with me,” she said. She has also continued to hope that one day she will be able to see.The hope of seeing the worldFor years, Vijayalakshmi has explored possible treatments for her condition. She travelled to the US for treatment in 2019, but the process was interrupted by the Covid-19 pandemic and questions over whether the treatment could actually restore her sight.Doctors, she has said, have differed over whether the problem lies with her retina or her brain. Despite the uncertainty, the desire has remained.She has spoken about wanting to see the world she has known primarily through voices, sounds and touch. That hope exists alongside an acceptance of the life she has built without sight. Her career has not waited for a cure, nor has she put her ambitions on hold.The National Award is the latest recognition of that life. But there was another part of her personal journey in which she also had to decide what she wanted- and what she would no longer accept.‘I don't have to tolerate all this’Vijayalakshmi has spoken candidly about the end of her marriage and described it as one of the saddest periods of her life. She said her former husband did not support her music and restricted the hours during which she could sing.“He didn't even agree to give rhythm for my music,” she said. “He even restricted my singing to some hours.” For someone whose independence had been built around music, the restrictions became increasingly difficult.Eventually, she chose to leave. “But I realized that I don't have to love tolerating all this and separated,” she said. Importantly, she described the decision as her own. “I made that decision. Neither father nor mother said to do so. Life decisions are in their own hands and cannot be given to anyone else.”A National Award, but not the end of the journeyVijayalakshmi’s National Award brings her career into focus, but her story is not simply about overcoming blindness to become a successful singer.It is also about the everyday negotiations that come with being a person with a disability- the frustration of being tested, the hurt of being excluded from ordinary experiences, the uncertainty surrounding treatment and the determination to make personal decisions independently.Her award-winning song tells people to rise, break barriers and conquer the world. For Vijayalakshmi, those words are not merely lyrics.“I, too, have overcome countless obstacles to reach where I am today,” she said.

articles.title: Trump welcomes Xi to Washington as US, China agree to extend trade truce
articles.summary: Trump takes rare step of meeting foreign leader at the airport, underscoring significance of US-China relationship.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping to Washington, DC, for a three-day visit and high-stakes talks on trade, Taiwan and artificial intelligence.

Xi’s landed at Joint Base Andrews, outside the US capital, on Wednesday as the Trump administration announced that the two countries have agreed to extend an 11-month trade deal that offered temporary relief from punishing tariffs.

Trump took the rare step of personally meeting Xi on his arrival, marking the first time in 11 years that a US president has greeted a foreign leader at the base, according to US media.

At the arrival ceremony, the leaders and their wives shook hands, spoke for a few minutes and stood for pictures as a military band played, cannons blasted and a B-1 military bomber flew overhead.

In a written statement afterwards, Xi said China and the US should be partners and not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. “He said that the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, complement each other and benefit the world,” Xinhua reported.

Trump’s in-person greeting signals the significance that Washington ascribes to its relationship with Beijing , whose meteoric economic rise over the last several decades has transformed it into a global superpower capable of rivalling the US.

Xi’s visit comes after he hosted Trump in Beijing in May.

His schedule in Washington, DC, will include a state dinner attended by leaders of the US’s powerful tech industry , a military ceremony at the White House and a visit to the National Archives, home to documents of historical and cultural significance such as the US Constitution and the Declaration of Independence.

His talks with Trump are likely to cover the US-Israel war on Iran, the US-China trade deal, AI , and US ties to Taiwan , the self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory, according to analysts.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Wednesday that he had met with Chinese ‌Vice Premier He Lifeng ahead of Xi’s visit to “see if we could ⁠do a bigger deal as opposed to just a series ⁠of smaller things”.

“We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan Agreement,” Bessent said.

The agreement, which was set to expire on November 10, has now been extended to January 10, he said.

Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, said the short extension suggests the two nations were planning a wider deal.

“The two sides indeed have a bigger scope of negotiation coming to their trade deals, and they need more time to negotiate the technicalities,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that the truce was expected to hold even before the trip began.

Sun called Xi’s visit to the US “unprecedented”, saying “there has never been any precedent in the history of US-China relations for the top two leaders of the two countries to visit each other within a single year”. She described the stabilisation of ties as “quite prominent and very impressive”, noting that only 12 months ago, the two countries were escalating tariffs and export controls against each other.

On Taiwan, Sun said Beijing’s main goal would be to prevent or stall a $14bn arms package that Congress approved earlier this year, but the Trump administration has been unwilling to advance.

She said she expected the most progress on AI, where the two governments could agree on ways to manage their dialogue.

“We know that the US has proposed a hotline mechanism for notification to each other when there is a significant security risk associated with AI that happens in their individual country,” she said. “We’ll have to see whether the two leaders are able to make progress on this important issue.”

articles.title: Local Virginia GOP chair says Arlington County officials prioritize illegal immigrants over public safety
articles.summary: Arlington County's sanctuary policies face sharp criticism in a House Judiciary Committee report over its limits on federal immigration enforcement.
articles.body: A recently released House Judiciary Committee report on one Virginia county's effort to resist the Trump administration's immigration enforcement agenda clashes with the region's deep blue politics, according to local Republicans. The 23-page interim staff report from the committee's Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement heavily criticized Arlington County's sanctuary policies, accusing the county and local Democratic-run jurisdictions of ignoring public safety while advocating policies that make it harder for federal immigration authorities to detain and arrest undocumented immigrants with criminal records. "Chairman [Jim] Jordan's Judiciary Committee report about Arlington is spot on," Matthew Hurtt, chairman of the Arlington County Republican Committee, told Fox News Digital. "Arlington elected officials prioritize illegal aliens over the safety of Arlington residents. And as an Arlington resident, I've seen this play out over the last several months." LOCAL GOP LEADER SLAMS $50K TAXPAYER 'SLUSH FUND' FOR FAMILIES OF DETAINED, DEPORTED IMMIGRANT BREADWINNERS The report noted the limited cooperation between local law enforcement and immigration authorities. It cited Arlington County's official board Trust Policy rules governing local law enforcement. The updated May 2025 Trust Policy prohibits the Arlington County Police Department "from initiating contact with federal immigration authorities" even when identifying an undocumented immigrant as a "violent felon, gang member, human trafficker, or terrorist." VIRGINIA COUNTY TO PAY UP TO $2K TO FAMILIES WITH PRIMARY WAGE EARNER DETAINED BY ICE In addition, the committee report referred to a July 16, 2026 closed-door deposition in which Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the Commonwealth’s Attorney for Arlington County and the City of Falls Church, acknowledged that her office considers immigration status when determining case outcomes and admitted that written guidelines do not forbid considering immigration status for any crime. She also defended a memo asking prosecutors to consider other charges when a Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipient is accused of drunk driving. SOROS-BACKED DA ACCUSED OF GOING EASY ON ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS GETS SQUEEZED BY HOUSE GOP Since U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services classifies a DUI conviction as a "significant misdemeanor," which bars DACA renewal and triggers deportation, the memo instructs prosecutors to consider DACA status to avoid "disproportionate and devastating collateral consequences." "It's not the job of a prosecutor to decide lenience against illegal aliens who are oftentimes committing violent crimes against individuals or property crimes, but that is exactly what Arlington Commonwealth's Attorney Parisa Dehghani-Tafti has been doing," Hurtt said. JIM JORDAN SUBPOENAS BLUE STATE DAS ACCUSED OF 'PREFERENTIAL TREATMENT' FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIMINALS "[Dehghani-]Tafti sees herself as a left-wing criminal justice activist," Hurtt added, criticizing Steve Descano, the Commonwealth's Attorney for nearby Democratic-run Fairfax County, which has made national headlines amid a string of crimes allegedly committed by undocumented immigrants. In a statement obtained by ARLNow, Dehghani-Tafti described the committee report as a "political sham." "The committee refused to hear my testimony in public because open testimony doesn’t let you distort a record," she said. "This report is the predictable product of that process— a piece of political propaganda timed for the midterms, built on the deliberate misrepresentations of my policies and my testimony. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Now it’s clear why they wouldn’t hold a public hearing and why they stonewalled my requests for the full deposition transcript," she added. "They didn’t want the public to see it. I demand the committee release the full, unedited transcript of my deposition immediately." Fox News Digital has reached out to Dehghani-Tafti's office, as well as the Sheriff's Office and the County Board.

articles.title: 'Proteinflation': Meet the people paying up to £100 for a bag of protein
articles.summary: Consumers are feeling the squeeze from the rising price of protein.
articles.body:
Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16.

The 30-year-old, who lives in London and works in banking, started going to the gym at a time when he says protein supplements were mostly associated with bodybuilders.

Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive.

He says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020.

By last year, the price had gone up to £120, though he managed to get one from eBay for £90.

Among his gym friends, the rising prices have even been given a nickname – "proteinflation".

Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base, while food manufacturers now offer high-protein versions of everything from bagels to water.

Evie Lewis is a more recent buyer of protein powder.

The 19-year-old University of Manchester student began using it a few months ago because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet.

"You hear a lot more about protein now on social media," she says.

But at £32.99 for a 420g tub, she's feeling the high price and tries to make the product stretch.

"I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested," she admits.

Max Longman, 32, from Manchester, works in real estate and has been taking protein supplements for 10 years, originally to help him gain weight.

He now drinks a protein shake every day and says his monthly spending on whey protein has risen from around £45 a year ago to £60 now.

"Loads of foods have protein added to them now. Up until a few years ago, I'd never heard of high-protein yoghurt, and now I eat it three or four times a week," he says.

More recently, weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have added another source of demand.

People taking these drugs typically eat less, and are often encouraged to make sure they get enough protein while losing weight to help preserve muscle.

But that growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem - supply has not kept pace.

And the result has been a sharp rise in the wholesale price of some key ingredients, and consumers are feeling the squeeze.

High whey protein prices take chunk out of THG profits

Food firms scramble to meet the high-protein craze

According to global market intelligence platform Expana, the European price of one widely used type of high-protein whey was 130% higher in late August than a year earlier, and more than four times its level three years ago.

There is no equivalent UK measure, but Expana says the UK market is closely linked to mainland Europe, where some British businesses source their whey protein.

Other dairy proteins have also become more expensive, with another type of whey protein up 60% over the year, while one type of milk protein concentrate was up 80%.

Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment.

So some are starting to adapt what they make, by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein.

Warrior, a UK sports nutrition company, is one of those looking for alternatives.

"Our whey protein powder was £12.50 on the shelf last year. We've put that up to £17.99 and we're still subsidising that from other aspects of the business," says its founder Kieran Fisher.

The company is now launching a product using other sources of protein, which Fisher says costs around half as much as whey.

The effects are also being felt outside the fitness market.

Dairy proteins are used in infant formula, and Expana says higher dairy protein costs have contributed to price rises there too.

There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust.

Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago.

For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max.

"It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says.

"If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly."

But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story.

"It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says.

Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag.

articles.title: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
articles.summary: Texas is now the country's biggest producer of solar-farmed electricity.
articles.body:
Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953.

Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father.

But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm.

Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight.

"I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says.

Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on.

Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm.

"Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing.

The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life."

Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms.

And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association.

He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population.

Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%, making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation.

"We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says.

Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state.

"No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says.

Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free.

"We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long.

By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration.

Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land.

Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent.

Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says.

Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth.

BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property.

He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries.

David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required.

"We're destroying the world as we're trying to save it," Truesdale says of the land clearing he has seen. He also points to the large lithium-ion battery units installed alongside many solar farms, drawing a comparison to fires that have occasionally engulfed similar batteries in electric bikes.

"If one of those things catches fire, they go off in series, so each one will progressively cause another one to go off," he says.

Both men say their objections are not about politics. Franklin County is solidly conservative, but its residents helped push through one of the state's first county-level moratoriums on new solar construction, before it was later rescinded under legal pressure from developers.

Their complaints echo a broader unease that has followed solar's expansion into rural Texas - worries about visual impact, water runoff after land is cleared, and battery storage units that scorch their land.

President Trump has called solar and wind power "farmer destroying" and moved to unwind tax credits for renewable projects.

Yet Fabrizio Lee and Associates, the polling firm used by President Trump, found back in February that 68% of Republican voters believe the country needs "all forms of electricity generation, including utility solar" to keep costs down.

Stover says he has found broad support in the Republican-controlled Texas state legislature. "There is an acceptance that these technologies bring reliability benefits to the grid," he says.

Back in Uvalde, Steve Cargil says that while he has no plans to retire any time soon, he is more positive that the farm might make it to a fifth generation after all, now that the solar farm has put a floor under its finances.

"You're better off being lucky than being smart," Cargil says, echoing something his father used to tell him. "And this was one of those cases where I was just lucky."

articles.title: Dopamine sites: India and the world are discovering the thrill of shopping without buying
articles.summary: Dopamine sites mimic shopping’s thrill without the spending, turning the ritual of consumption into a digital game.
articles.body:
You are hungry. Or you are not. It doesn't matter.

You open FoodNeverComes, pick from 22 cuisines and start scrolling. Butter chicken looks good. So does bibimbap. You add a few dishes, watch the total climb and hit checkout. A tracker says a rider is on the way.

Then you get a dummy AI-generated call from inside the site. He is outside your building, he says, but cannot find your street or door. Except there was never any food in the first place. The order exists only on the screen.

"Order the food. Skip the bill," says the site. Its slogan is blunter: "The food never comes - but the dopamine does."

Built by two 26-year-old software developers - Purvansh Parmar and Anshul Sharma - from Udaipur in India's northern state of Rajasthan, FoodNeverComes says it has attracted more than 2.7m visitors since its launch in June.

It now offers 22 kitchens, 327 dishes and 319 real recipes, complete with fake prices, a simulated checkout and a fictional delivery experience.

FoodNeverComes belongs to a new internet genre: "dopamine sites", which recreate the rituals of consumption without the consumption. There are fake shopping sites, fake delivery services and even fake holidays.

The genre took off in South Korea and has since travelled well beyond, spawning a growing crop of sites - Dopamine Shop or Fakehaul , for example - that mimic everything from food delivery and shopping to travel.

What, exactly, are we enjoying when we enjoy buying something?

The idea began with the founders' own shopping habits. Parmar and Sharma met on a computer science diploma course and later started NeuroX AI, which builds software and AI products and makes Instagram content. They noticed it in their own lives: online baskets filling up with things they wanted, but never actually bought.

Sharma would browse electronics, fill an online basket and abandon it. Parmar's mother did much the same. "She would add things to the cart and say, 'I will order this later'," he recalls.

Parmar's own version ended at food delivery checkouts. During a two-month project in Mumbai, he says, he was spending 5,000-10,000 rupees a week on food, sometimes ordering treats he did not necessarily need: Belgian waffles, ice cream and, once, a large jar of sour cream he barely wanted and gave away to friends.

He believes "perhaps the real craving was not always for the food, but for the ritual of ordering it".

What begins as genuine hunger, the two argue, can become associated with the pleasure of ordering. Over time, boredom, anxiety or habit can trigger the urge even when the hunger has disappeared.

"Sometimes you're not hungry at all. You're bored or busy, and then you realise that ordering food makes you feel good. You start associating the act of ordering with that dopamine hit. Eventually, it's not just the food you want," says Parmar.

Ravi Dhar, director of the Yale Center for Customer Insights, calls this "anticipatory utility" - the pleasure of looking forward to consumption. It is especially strong with things that capture the imagination - a new pair of shoes, a holiday, a restaurant meal - because anticipation becomes part of the experience.

Sometimes, Dhar says, anticipation can be more pleasurable than ownership: "The thrill is in the chase." Once the object is acquired and the tension resolved, psychological arousal falls.

Neuroscience has a name for this gap between the chase and the catch, and it complicates a popular idea. Dopamine is not simply the brain's pleasure chemical, whatever the internet's talk of "dopamine hits" might suggest.

Kent Berridge, a University of Michigan neuroscientist who developed the theory of "wanting" and "liking", says they are separate processes. Wanting is the motivational pull towards something; liking is the pleasure of having it. They often travel together, but not always. Dopamine, in his account, drives the first, not the second.

Tempting food or products online are likely to activate this wanting system, which Berridge calls "incentive salience".

"Some situations can trigger 'wanting' by itself," he says. We can pursue something intensely even when the eventual pleasure is weak - or, in more everyday terms, want something more than we ultimately like it.

Dr Anna Lembke, a Stanford University addiction psychiatrist and author of Dopamine Nation, makes a similar distinction.

"To call dopamine a chemical of pleasure is an oversimplification," she told me. "Dopamine is the molecule that says 'get more of' or 'do more of', but it doesn't necessarily equate to pleasure."

What she adds is the role of ritual. Cues and habits attached to a reward can become reinforcing in their own right, she says: in addiction, the routines leading up to drug use can eventually matter as much as the drug itself. "Anticipation of reward can be as reinforcing as the reward itself," she says.

Can repeatedly ordering imaginary food satisfy a real craving? Berridge says the ritual could produce a "dopamine hit and strong 'wanting', and also evoke faint conditioned 'liking'".

But he would expect the "novelty to soon wear off", and would be "surprised" if many people returned to place more than about 10 imaginary orders.

Dhar is more open to the possibility that simulated consumption could serve as a kind of release valve.

"While we still need more empirical data to know if simulated shopping can satisfy a consumer urge, evidence from simulated consumption in gaming shows it can be highly effective," he says.

But there is an equally plausible danger: the ritual may simply rehearse the behaviour it is supposed to replace.

Lembke says the evidence is not in yet, and the effect may depend on the person. But her own bet is that, over time, the sites could "reinforce the same addictive neural networks they are trying to simulate".

"The one up side, though, is that people using these sites have on some level already admitted to themselves they have a problem, and that admission is often the first step in recovery," says Lembke.

Sharma ran an accidental experiment of his own. When his phone screen cracked, he spent a week on Amazon comparing six or seven replacements and adding them to his basket. Then he repaired the handset.

"I enjoyed the process of research and putting the phones in the cart," he says. "Eventually I didn't buy a phone."

He now catches himself doing the same on food delivery sites, particularly when anxious, filling baskets without checking out. "I realised that I suffer from this problem," he says.

The site's blog explores the "serious side" of the fake takeaway, from food-delivery addiction and why fake ordering feels good to cravings, guilt and the psychology of the shopping cart.

The founders have since taken the idea beyond food. A second site, TripNeverLeaves, lets users plan a holiday - destination, flight, seat, hotel and activities - then sends them on a virtual flight that never leaves the runway. They say it has attracted more than 100,000 visitors.

Who those visitors are is harder to establish. But Lembke says younger people may be especially vulnerable to reinforcing digital rewards because the "developing brain is a vulnerable brain".

"In childhood and early adolescence, the front lobe, which acts like the brakes on appetite, is not yet fully connected to the emotion centres of the brain. Hence, teens are more likely to take risks without appreciating the negative consequences, and more likely to get addicted to reinforcing substances and behaviours, once exposed," she says.

For now, the founders say the sites are not about making money. They plan to keep them free and eventually share the data with neuroscientists and psychologists.

What looks like a joke about ordering too much food has stumbled into a bigger question about modern consumption: if so much of the thrill comes before we get the thing, do we need the thing at all?

articles.title: Antrim: 'I had to learn to walk again after hit and run crash'
articles.summary: Fiona McGill suffered a shattered pelvis, two broken vertebrae and a broken leg, and wakes up in pain every day.
articles.body:
When Fiona Gill was struck by a van she was left with a shattered pelvis, two broken vertebrae and a broken leg.

The mother of two said she still wakes up in pain every day.

"It was two major surgeries, four months in a wheelchair, and I had to learn to walk again," she said.

Antrim GAA footballer Kavan Keenan, who was driving the van in October 2024, was recently handed a nine month suspended prison sentence and a 12 month driving ban.

Speaking for the first time since the crash, McGill recounted her injuries and the painful recovery.

"My hip needed pinned, my pelvis was shattered, they pulled a piece of car bumper out of my thigh which had cut my muscle away," she said.

"The pain was horrendous because I had injuries on every side. The nurses had to turn me [in my bed] and the pain was excruciating."

McGill's relatives had to take care of her young boys while she was recovering.

"I spent five weeks in hospital, so my sisters had to take a child each. I had to essentially parent from my hospital bed.

"My eldest was doing his GCSEs so the impact on him has been significant."

Keenan left the scene and initially denied driving the vehicle after the crash in Martinstown, County Antrim, but changed his plea one month before he was due to go on trial.

The 27-year-old from Millfield in Ballymena admitted injuring the woman by careless driving and failing to remain at the scene of an accident.

He also admitted to driving without insurance and failing to report an accident.

The footballer's father was given a community service order for trying to take the blame .

Asked about the sentence Keenan received, McGill said elements of it were incredibly disappointing.

"In terms of his driving, he should have got a bigger ban and he should be retested again," she said.

"I wouldn't want his children, or his child, to go through what my children went through, having their parent taken away.

"But I feel like his lack of remorse throughout this whole process needed more of a punishment."

The judge said there were a number of aggravating factors in the case against Keenan, including his failure to identify himself as the driver at the time.

During sentencing, the judge said "a common theme" in the character references was Keenan's remorse, and he also highlighted the defendant's contribution to his community.

McGill disagrees and said she feels his "remorse is only for himself".

"He has shown me no remorse," she said. "Our barrister said in court there had been none shown."

McGill said she was speaking now because she wanted people to know the true impact of the crash.

"Different people in my community would ask me how my leg was. The truth was it was so much more.

"I wake up every day in pain. It has completely changed my life."

You can hear Fiona McGill's interview in full on BBC Radio Ulster's Evening Extra at 17:00 BST.

articles.title: Bessent reveals extension to Busan agreement with China until January
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent outlines three ways the Iran war could end while warning Tehran is a "cornered animal" running out of options.
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that United States and Chinese officials agreed to extend their bilateral trade truce known as the "Busan agreement" Wednesday on Fox News. The Busan agreement was set down by President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 and is a trade-war truce intended to ease economic tension between the two nations. "We have agreed today that we will extend what we call the Busan agreement, the economic détente between the two countries that was scheduled to end on Nov. 10 that is going to be extended until Jan. 10 to give us more time to see what we can do on the economic front," Bessent told "Special Report." As the United States’ war with Iran nears the seventh-month mark, Bessent is outlining three possible ways the conflict could end while warning that the regime is a "cornered animal." Bessent said the conflict could end in three ways: members of the regime turn on one another, the Iranian people revolt or Tehran finally comes to the negotiating table and reaches an agreement. "One, the regime turns on each other — not impossible," he told Fox News. "Two, we get some kind of uprising for the Iranian people. They've probably killed 50,000 of their own population, so very difficult. And then three, to get the Iranians to, if they want to make a deal, to stick to the deal." AFTER 6 MONTHS OF WAR, US MUST PREPARE FOR A FUTURE AFTER IRAN’S GOVERNMENT FALLS The Treasury Department is continuing its sweeping economic pressure campaign against Iran, targeting Iranian assets and financial networks while pressuring foreign governments and businesses to sever economic ties with Tehran — an effort Bessent said the "world has never seen." "We have an effort never seen before in terms of constricting and cutting off the financial oxygen to them," the Treasury chief said. "And I don't know whether it's gonna be a week, a month or two months, but they're going to yell uncle." BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY The Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August. It is an extension of the economic strangulation campaign aimed at further severing Iran’s financial lifelines sustaining the regime and further isolating Tehran from the global financial system. "We have made it very clear around the world, whether it's the financiers, the people who are doing business, the people who are supplying the Iranians, we know who you are, you know who you are, and we are going to prosecute and execute your companies and your bank accounts every day and every week," Bessent warned. The Treasury chief said he is "not sure" how Iranian officials attending the United Nations General Assembly will return home after imposing hefty restrictions on Iranian airlines. "External flights from Iran, probably more than 80 or 90% of them, got shut down. I'm not sure how the Iranian representatives at the UN are gonna get home," he told Fox News. WALTZ DELIVERS BLUNT WARNING TO NATIONS DEFYING IRAN SANCTIONS, TOUTS GREENLAND DEAL Bessent, who dismissed reports suggesting he is Trump’s top pick for AI czar, addressed his multi-day talks with China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng this week. The secretary proposed an AI "notification mechanism" between the United States and China that would allow the two countries to alert each other about AI-related safety incidents that could pose national security risks. "They're very eager to engage with us on AI because… the U.S. is substantially in the lead, China's behind us," Bessent said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It's very important for us to engage on this," he continued. "I think we are working to define with them what we think the most important or the most perilous risk factors are, whether it's uncontrolled AI agents, whether it is non-state actors using AI, either for cyber ops or for biologics."

articles.title: 5 crucial issues lawmakers want Trump to address with China
articles.summary: President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold a series of high-stakes meetings in Washington, marking the first official state visit by China’s leader in more than a decade. The meetings come at a fragile moment in relations between the U.S. and Beijing, which have spent the better part of the last two years…
articles.body:
President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold a series of high-stakes meetings in Washington, marking the first official state visit by China’s leader in more than a decade.

The meetings come at a fragile moment in relations between the U.S. and Beijing, which have spent the better part of the last two years embroiled in a drag-out trade war sparked by Trump’s global tariffs.

Trade will be front and center, as the two superpowers are expected to discuss ways to stabilize agreements and ease the economic volatility that’s accompanied the retaliatory feud. But it’s hardly the only hot-button issue on the menu this week.

Trump and Xi are also facing pressure to tackle safety concerns surrounding artificial intelligence amid growing concerns about catastrophic risk. Beijing’s role in propping up Tehran in the middle of the Iran war is also sure to be on the table. And some lawmakers want Trump to press Xi on China’s dismal human rights record and the importance of preserving Taiwanese autonomy.

Trump greeted Xi upon his arrival on Wednesday evening at Joint Base Andrews, just outside Washington, and more formal meetings are scheduled at the White House over the next two days, including an official state dinner on Thursday night and a private tea on Friday morning. Xi will also visit the National Archives to view America’s founding documents, marking a continuation of Trump’s rolling celebration of the country’s 250th birthday.

Here are five issues that lawmakers in the Capitol want Trump to press in his talks with Xi.

The AI debate has always been accompanied by warnings that the technology, if not harnessed carefully, could pose an existential threat to humankind . But the urgency surrounding that threat was heightened enormously by recent statements from several leaders of the AI industry who said the danger was not only real but might also be imminent.

It’s also global, since every superpower is involved in the artificial intelligence arms race. And with that in mind, lawmakers on Capitol Hill want Trump to work with Xi this week on some form of global commitment to adopt new limits on AI development.

“This visit from China presents a perfect opportunity to establish a formal, and probably permanent, dialogue between the U.S. and China around AI safety issues — to put that process in place now so that we can start working towards some agreements and understandings to protect the world from AI risks,” said Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.).

Trump has been cold to the idea of adopting limits on the technology, saying such restrictions would only hobble U.S. companies in the race against countries like China. But that, some lawmakers said, is only more reason for an international pact that would level the field for everyone.

“For those who don’t want national standards you could still make the case that we need the international standards,” Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) said.

Van Hollen — along with 16 other senators — spearheaded a letter this week, pressing Trump to broach the topic with Xi. And others have gotten even more specific in recommending reforms.

In the last Congress, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) had championed a law designed to prohibit AI systems from launching nuclear weapons without a human hand directing the process. He wants China to adopt a similar safeguard.

“I urge Trump to ask the Chinese leader to also commit that they’re never going to let AI launch a nuclear weapon by itself,” Lieu said.

The trade war between the U.S. and China escalated to such a point last year that the tariffs on some goods, applied by both sides, soared well above 100 percent . The tensions have eased since those heights, mitigated by a series of agreements that scaled back those levies.

But tariffs remain one of Trump’s favorite tools in conducting foreign affairs. And the president frequently voices his frustrations with a trade deficit with China, which topped $1 trillion last year.

Those tensions will form the backdrop of this week’s summit, where both leaders will be facing pressure to extend the temporary agreements that have provided some relief to businesses and consumers in both countries.

Heading into the meeting, Democrats are pressing Trump on a very specific trade issue, urging him to end the sale of sophisticated chips to China.

“We can’t take what Donald Trump and the White House says seriously about China when they are taking actions that are literally helping the Chinese Communist Party build out their AI systems by allowing U.S. companies to sell high-performance AI chips to China,” said Lieu. “There is no reason for that to happen.”

The long-standing threat to Taiwan, a self-governing island democracy that Beijing claims as its own, has united congressional lawmakers of both parties for decades. The threat has gained some urgency in recent years, fueling the push on Capitol Hill for the U.S. to stand as a line of defense against any Chinese effort to “unify” the two governments.

Xi’s visit, some hope, will be another opportunity for U.S. officials to send that message.

“We should make sure that President Trump understands who our adversaries are across the world, and who our allies have been,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters Wednesday in the Capitol.

“Taiwan is an ally, and hopefully Donald Trump is not going to give up Taiwanese autonomy or sovereignty or territorial integrity in ways that would be inconsistent with what past presidents — whether they are Democrats or Republicans — have done.”

In an effort not to confront Chinese leaders directly on the contentious topic, U.S. administrations of both parties have, for decades, adopted a fragile and hazy approach to Taiwan’s political standing, known as “strategic ambiguity.”

Still, the Pentagon provides billions of dollars in arms to Taiwan. And a recent delay in the delivery of some of those weapons sparked an outcry from Republicans on Wednesday, coinciding with Xi’s arrival in Washington.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) — accompanied by three other Republican senators — wrote to top administration officials urging the release of those funds.

“It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities,” the four GOP senators wrote .

Some observers have warned that Trump’s approach to the Russia-Ukraine conflict — especially his sporadic push to have Kyiv cede certain seized territories to Moscow as a condition of ending the war — sends the dangerous signal to Beijing that the U.S. would be willing to accept a Chinese takeover of the sovereign island state.

“Everyone’s fearful that Xi Jinping is going to move on Taiwan. All you have to do is look at what happened in Hong Kong, what they do to kind of control their population,” said Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.). “I know Trump is often enamored with that.”

Amid America’s opioid addiction epidemic, much of the focus has been on drug smugglers operating south of the border, including in Mexico as well as in Central and South America — a dynamic that fueled the Trump administration’s extraordinary attacks on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean Sea.

Yet by the administration’s own accounting, China-based manufacturing companies remain the primary source of the fentanyl building blocks and other precursor chemicals that have fueled the production of synthetic opioids.

In response, the Treasury Department has slapped sanctions on some Chinese chemical companies. But heading into this week’s summit, some lawmakers want Beijing to go much further to police those manufacturers on their own.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) is one of them. He broached that topic with Xi during a visit with the Chinese leader in 2023, which yielded some results, Schumer said, “but not close to enough.”

Schumer said Wednesday on the Senate floor that Trump must push Xi “to do more to crack down synthetic opioid precursors.”

“Trump ought to take legal action against those opioid precursors that have already been scheduled to come in here and crack down on illicit finance schemes keeping this deadly trade going,” he continued.

“As I said … China’s made some steps in the right direction, but it needs to do much more,” the senator noted, referring to comments he made during his 2023 meeting with the Chinese leader.

Lawmakers in both parties have long challenged Chinese leaders on their bleak history of human rights abuses, whether directed at Tibetan separatists, ethnic Uyghurs, Beijing critics in Hong Kong or pro-democracy advocates anywhere.

That protest movement was energized ahead of Xi’s visit in Washington, where activists staged demonstrations against the Chinese president on the grounds of the Capitol, and lawmakers pushed Trump to broach the thorny issue when the pair of leaders meet.

Rep. Jim McGovern (D-Mass.), who stands among Congress’s most vocal critics of Beijing’s human rights record, is leading the charge. He and Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) spearheaded two letters to Trump urging the president to make the issue of political prisoners and other human rights abuses a priority during the visit.

“Even a single mention of a detainee’s name by a senior U.S. official, let alone by yourself, can significantly increase that individual’s chances of clemency or improved treatment,” the pair of Democrats wrote.

On Wednesday, McGovern continued that push, staging a press conference just outside the Capitol, along with other human rights activists who called for the release of thousands of political detainees.

articles.title: I didn't know my partner was raping me while I slept
articles.summary: Adelle Overton had been with Steven Uden for 13 years when she found out he had been raping her.
articles.body:
"In my eyes, up until maybe the day before he admitted to what he'd done, it was the best relationship I've ever had."

Adelle Overton's boyfriend of 13 years, Steven Uden, appeared to be the perfect partner.

They met on the set of a zombie film and had lots of shared interests. She says Uden was kind and loving and even gave up work to be Overton's carer when she became disabled.

"He was wonderful. I loved him deeply, and I think I still kind of do a bit," says Overton, sitting on a sofa at her home in Derby.

Overton trusted Uden, but that trust was shattered when he admitted he had been raping her while she slept.

"I instantly felt betrayed. I'd never felt so safe in a relationship before that point," says Overton.

Uden had cared for Overton while she was being treated for breast cancer, but he later told police he had raped her while she was under the effects of the medication.

"That sense of betrayal, that I thought I knew him, but I don't know who he was," says Overton.

"And the thought that he'd been living with me for 13 years, he helped raise my children.

Uden is now in prison, and Overton has decided to talk about what happened in the hope it will help others.

Overton and Uden met in 2009, during the filming of a zombie film being shot in Nottingham, when she was 29 and he was 27.

Uden was doing make-up and acting, and Overton was one of the actors too. They were both in relationships with other people but stayed in touch as friends.

They eventually became a couple on 13 January 2012 - Overton remembers the date because they had a Friday the 13th film marathon.

Overton said being with Uden felt different from the relationships she had been in in the past.

"He was fun and caring and I felt loved by him," she says.

They had met in an unconventional way, and their life together was unconventional too. They worked as professional zombies for a company that ran zombie survival horror experience days.

Playing a zombie required Overton to be physically active, but she eventually had to give it up in 2017 after being diagnosed with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome .

Uden then became her carer towards the start of 2018.

"He did almost everything for me," she says.

Looking back, with hindsight, Overton - nicknamed Dell - thinks Uden did start to become controlling.

"He would enjoy telling everybody else what I was capable of doing," she says.

"Somebody would come up with a suggestion for doing something, he'd enjoy saying, 'I don't think Dell would be able to manage that, let's think of something else'."

But Overton now knows that Uden's behaviour was far more sinister than she could ever have imagined.

She had suspicions in 2020 while having chemotherapy for breast cancer.

"I don't know if the discomfort in my body was more apparent, but I woke up while he was doing it," she says.

"He made loads of excuses like, 'I thought you were awake, and you were making all the right noises'.

"I was thinking about all of the stress we were under, and he's saying he did it by accident."

"I guess it was easier to believe the lie than process what the truth might have been," she says.

But Overton started having difficulty sleeping.

"I think somewhere in there, in my head, my brain just didn't feel safe while I was asleep," she says.

Overton says she also struggled to be intimate with Uden, and started having more nightmares relating to her past experience of sexual abuse.

"At the time I thought I was linking it to my trauma, and I was judging him and what he'd done more harshly because of my trauma," she says.

"I started to feel guilty and started berating myself internally for it all."

Uden didn't confess until five years later, in 2025, when he was having cancer treatment himself - for bowel cancer.

"I think something must have been playing on his mind, because now he was seeing what I was going through from the other side," Overton says.

"He definitely lingered on the fact that he didn't look after me very well when I was going through treatment."

This brought back Overton's memory from five years before, of waking up and finding Uden having sex with her.

She says: "I pushed him. 'What do you mean by that? What do you mean you didn't look after me? In what way?'"

At some point during the conversation, which Overton says was spread over two days, Uden phoned a friend and admitted what he had done, before returning home and confessing to Overton.

She felt betrayed, and sickened, but did not immediately end the relationship. She felt like she relied upon Uden, and she loved him too.

Overton was already having group therapy for past sexual abuse and mentioned it during her next session.

She says: "It was one of the counsellors, one of the therapists that shook me out of it, because I was in bits, I was in floods of tears saying, 'what do I do? How do I stop him from doing it?'

"And she said, 'you kick him out and you call the police'. And later on that day she said they'd had a safeguarding meeting, and they would be calling the police about the whole thing, and at that point I kind of knew that it was out of my hands."

The case was allocated to Det Sgt Eleanor Kirton, of Derbyshire Police.

"The first thing I did was contact Adelle," she says.

"Understandably she was incredibly distressed about what had happened."

After interviewing Overton, police arrested Uden.

"When I interviewed him, he immediately confessed to what he'd done," says Eleanor.

"He straight away admitted that he had raped her, which is very unusual for our investigations to go down that route so quickly."

Uden was charged with two counts of rape, which he later pleaded guilty to in court, and was given a prison sentence of six years and eight months.

Kirton says Overton's actions have helped protect other women.

"Her bravery and resilience has meant that we've safeguarded so many other people, that this person could have continued doing these offences to," she adds.

"If someone feels that this might be happening to them, I would really encourage them to come and speak to us about it, because there are things we can do, and this proves that."

But Overton still struggles to understand why her supposedly loving partner of 13 years would rape her while she slept.

"I don't know how somebody can get pleasure out of somebody not reacting, and that was the thing that just did not make sense to me," she says.

"He had a preference, I don't know how to put it, for sleeping women.

"He wanted me to be asleep, and he wanted me to not be aware of what he was doing."

Overton suspects Uden was drugging her with her own medication, which he had full control of.

"I had little pill pots, and he'd pop all of my meds out for me," she says.

"I've now got a lot less of the sedative medication than other medications, so I strongly suspect he was overdosing me to try and keep me asleep."

Kirton says it was what police call a "historic case", so forensics and toxicology would not have been able to confirm whether or not this had happened.

Also, there was not any evidence about this presented in court.

But Uden did tell police he had raped Overton on one occasion while she was having chemotherapy, which makes people more tired.

Kirton says: "I think he actually introduced it at the time, saying she was having chemotherapy, and he accepts that she would have been under the influence of the medication when it happened on that occasion."

While Uden was charged with raping Overton on two occasions, she believes he has done so more times.

"He told me he'd done it to me seven or eight times," says Overton.

Her daughter, Shari Overton, says it has been difficult to see the impact Uden's crimes have had on her mum.

"She's very different now. I can see her confidence has dropped massively," says Shari.

"I'm also incredibly proud of her for going through with this and talking to the police and the court and standing up for herself."

Overton hopes her story will show other vulnerable people they do not need to tolerate abuse at the hands of their so-called carers.

"I feel like I need to speak out, because it got me thinking about how many other disabled people are in situations where somebody has got control over them," she says.

"I used to think for a few months after I found everything out, that maybe it was some kind of payment for his care. Maybe I owed him that intimacy. But I didn't and nobody else does either."

articles.title: Sunny Hostin reveals she was holdout juror in 1991 ‘Butcher of Tompkins Square Park’ trial
articles.summary: Hostin said on “The View” that she changed her fellow jurors’ minds to find Daniel Rakowitz not criminally responsible by reason of insanity at his 1991 New York City trial.
articles.body: “The View” host Sunny Hostin revealed that she was the holdout juror in the high-profile “Butcher of Tompkins Square Park” trial in 1991. Hostin spoke about her time serving on that jury during a discussion about the Lindsay Clancy case, which ended this month in a mistrial with the jury split 11-1. “The reason I felt that I feel so strongly about this holdout juror is because I was a holdout juror in a case, in the Daniel Rakowitz case,” Hostin said on Tuesday’s episode, to the shock of her castmates. Rakowitz was accused of killing and dismembering Monika Beerle, a 26-year-old dance student, then boiling her body parts and feeding them in a soup to people in Tompkins Square Park in the East Village of Manhattan in 1989. He was found not guilty by reason of insanity at his 1991 trial, which dominated headlines. Hostin said she served on the jury before she went to law school. “When I brought it up at the Hot Topics meeting, I don’t think everyone believed me. And then my producer looked it up, and I’m in The New York Times,” she said. The show then aired a picture of a newspaper clipping from an old New York Times article that read: “Several jurors questioned afterward said one holdout juror was principally responsible for preventing them from returning a guilty verdict.” “That was me,” Hostin said. “It was because I saw clearly that he was psychotic. He was in psychosis. He did not mean to kill her, and once he killed her, he panicked. He chopped up her body parts. Yes, boiled her body parts. Tried to commit the perfect crime ... and he fed her body parts to the unhoused.” The jury deliberated for an intense nine days, and its talks were at times combative, Hostin recalled. “One juror threw a chair at me they were so angry with me. But one by one I picked them off and said: ‘What about this? What about that?’ And we ended up all 12 unanimously voting that he was not criminally responsible by reason of insanity,” she said. Rakowitz was ordered in 2010 to remain at maximum-security Kirby Forensic Psychiatric Center on Ward’s Island. Hostin noted that Rakowitz remains in a mental institution, which she called “a different type of prison.” Her castmates were stunned by Hostin’s revelation, some appearing to disagree with her position in the jury. Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin said, “And you got this guy off?” as Hostin described the grisly crime. Star Jones, who was seated next to Hostin, joked, “Excuse me, can I move over?” Speaking about the Clancy case, Hostin called Massachusetts’ insanity defense “well-established” and said she agreed Clancy was not criminally responsible by reason of insanity. Clancy’s defense argued she was not criminally responsible for killing her three children because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis. Some jurors have said one holdout juror did not want to acquit. That juror, Michael P. Desronvil, spoke out last week, saying in a statement, “Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses, and what the prosecution presented, I thought it was enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing and planned.”

articles.title: Why the Dutch dictionary has a new word for labia
articles.summary: Campaigners hope the new words will lead to less body shaming and more sex positivity.
articles.body:
Can you imagine seeing the words "shame lips" on your medical notes? The term, which can also be translated as "pubic lips", is the Dutch word for a women's body part. But, for some, it's just one of countless examples that are outdated and loaded with stigma.

Last month, leading Dutch dictionary Dikke van Dale said it would include a new term for the labia, "vulvalippen" - in its upcoming online addition - alongside the traditional term "schaamlippen".

European campaigners have long been calling for a rewrite of terms used to discuss women's bodies, sexuality and health. What unites them is the desire to move away from terms that are often seen as misogynistic or judgmental.

"Language shapes how we see ourselves," says Shari Klein, one of the founders of the Schaamteloos campaign, which targets words that use "schaam" or "shame".

"It's crucial people have a more neutral, anatomically correct word - not a word that links to shame, whether consciously or sub-consciously," she says.

Calls to use vulvalippen aren't new but campaigners say inclusion in the dictionary may be a sign society is "finally ready for change".

Esther Van der Valk, part of prominent Dutch feminist group Dolle Mina, says it's also about sex positivity and reducing body shaming.

The campaign's next steps are to convince doctors and officials to use vulvalippen in leaflets and consultations.

Ton den Boon, editor of the dictionary, says adding vulvalippen is justified because it is becoming more established in the language and is being used more in the media, biology text books, medical leaflets and is even seen in veterinary medicine.

But whether it will be adopted widely is yet to be seen.

Other Dutch words, relevant to both men and women, could carry similar connotations - from "schaam haar" (pubic or shame hair) or "schaam been" (pubic or shame bone) to even "schaam lice" for pubic lice.

However, critics say changing a word will not necessarily change people's lives.

Language around birth should be less judgemental

The campaign mirrors attempts in Germany, where in 2018 journalists Gunda Windmüller and Mithu Sanyal started a petition to change "Shamlippen" to "Vulvalippen".

Windmüller says she was compelled to after a gynaecologist told her of the shame some women carry when discussing their bodies and having medical examinations.

When writing her article, she realised she couldn't even mention anatomy without including the word shame.

"Vulvalippen" has not yet been adopted by a German dictionary, but Windmüller has spotted it in conversations, school textbooks and women's magazines.

Her hope is the Dutch move will ignite support closer to home.

Similarly, in Sweden a new word for "hymen" was added in the academic dictionary after a 2009 campaign.

The association for sexuality education (RFSU) felt traditional term "mödomshinna", which translates as maidenhood skin or virginity membrane, was anatomically inaccurate and did nothing to dispel myths around hymens and virginity.

The new term "slidkrans" translates as vaginal corona - reflecting the fact the hymen is often folds of tissue in a ring, rather than a seal that breaks once.

"With a new word we can challenge the myths that seek to control women's sexuality and freedom," Sonja Ghaderi of the RFSU says.

Ghaderi says slidkrans is used particularly by healthcare professionals and in youth clinics but adds misinformation still exists emphasising the "need to change social constructs".

In the UK, feminist podcast host Nicola Denson-Elliott started a petition to replace the word "hysterectomy" (surgical removal of the womb) with "uterectomy".

She argues, as others have, that hysterectomy has linguistic links with hysteria - once seen as a disease of emotional excess in women - and wants a more "anatomically correct term" not one "associated with emotion."

The petition describes it as "medical misogyny", adding: "Women deserve terminology that respects them."

Linguistics researcher Dr Beth Malory says any changes need to be researched first.

"Will people understand uterectomy? Is simply saying removal of the womb better?"

New words cannot be ambiguous, she says, it's important to look at the whole system so there is no confusion.

Malory also studies language around pregnancy and loss.

One phrase highlighted in her research is "incompetent cervix" used to describe the shortening of the cervix that can increase risks of pregnancy loss and early birth. Women told her it made them feel blamed for the medical issue.

"Why do we need judgmental words like failure or incompetence?" says obstetrician Dr Brooke Vandermolen .

Even though they appear in medical textbooks, she tells me she's moved away from certain terms, including "failure to progress" - which describes labour not moving forward as expected.

"Language is incredibly important and the words we choose can show recognition and make people feel validated and seen."

In 2022, the Royal College of Midwives produced guidance offering alternative phrases.

But Vandermolen says some traditional terms are still being used and still cause distress.

"I hope this change in the Netherlands sparks more conversations here about how we speak about women's bodies. What we say can have a lasting impact."
