articles.title: Oleshky: Residents eating garden weeds in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water
articles.summary: The BBC has spoken to residents in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky who say they are being "constantly shelled".
articles.body:
"Two more civilians died last night," says Halia, before her phone connection cuts off.

She is trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which she says is "constantly shelled" and cut off from food and water.

Three days later she tells me the two who were killed were a husband and wife. She knew them well.

They were bringing home a bag of food from the closest neighbouring town of Radensk, 23km (14 miles) away, but were unable to get home before a curfew imposed by Russian occupation authorities.

They were then killed by a drone. Four separate sources have confirmed the deaths of two civilians carrying food on 20 September.

Halia does not want to share their names for fear she might be identified. Her name has been changed to protect her safety.

Hers is just one of the many harrowing accounts the BBC has heard from residents in the front-line city in southern Kherson in recent days.

Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.

It is also one of the cities where thousands of people lost their homes after the collapse of Nova Khakova Dam in 2023 , flooding buildings up to their rooftops. Ukraine and Nato accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.

Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now the Ukrainian government estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

Residents say children remaining in wider Oleshky are suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services, and are "degrading" without access to education.

Many have also told the BBC independently there is only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.

Ukraine has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

To stay or risk the 'Road of Death' - Ukrainian civilians trapped in frontline city

Earlier this week the Kremlin acknowledged that Oleshky faced "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.

The local population is living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha.

Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Sybiha called on the international community to pressure Russia into allowing humanitarian aid into the city.

Inside Oleshky, Halia faces a daily struggle to survive.

"There is no food here in the city," she says, adding that the last food delivery was back in May.

"I eat once a day, a dinner only," she says. "I make some plain bread, sometimes I can have it with a tomato, or with some honey, and a tea. That's it."

Many residents have turned to cooking garden weeds as they have run out of the vegetables they managed to grow over the summer, she explains.

Which weeds are safe to eat and how to boil them has become a topic of discussion on local Telegram messaging chats, along with calls between residents to sell, swap or share pieces of food.

No shops are open any more in Oleshky, with residents unable to source either clothes or hygiene products. The city has had no electricity, gas or water since the Kakhovka dam was attacked three years ago.

While some residents have risked travelling on foot along mined roads out of the city in search of supplies, it is now deemed too much of a danger.

Working out how many people have been killed in Oleshky is difficult.

The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has recorded reports this year of at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and Hola Prystan - about 24km to the east.

Local volunteers estimate that number could be significantly higher.

Ksenia Arkhipova has been counting the dead since she managed to escape Oleshky in summer 2022 - a few months after it was taken by the Russian army.

She is a volunteer who is involved in attempts to deliver food and medicine and facilitating evacuations to Oleshky. Locals trust her with their sensitive personal information.

"I've been putting together a spreadsheet of all those who died as soon as I find out about it, with their names and dates of birth – I've got around 1,200 people now," she says. "Sometimes I don't have time to update it, as the list grows one or two people longer every day: someone was killed by a drone, someone else stepped on the landmine."

While the BBC cannot independently verify these figures, one local resident has given her personal account of losing her loved ones.

Both her parents were killed in Oleshky this summer, said Tetiana - also not her real name. She confirmed their identities to the BBC with their dates of birth and photos, but asked not to have them published for her own safety.

"They were shot inside their home. Russian soldiers came there and wanted to take it," she said.

Burying the bodies of people killed in Oleshky has been restricted by Russian occupation authorities, residents say. This has made counting the dead even harder.

They "do not allow us to bury the dead if they were killed by a drone, stepped on a landmine or were killed in any other way", said Tetiana.

Russia's occupation authorities demand those deaths are confirmed by post mortem examination carried out by a Russian doctor, the BBC has been told. That is not possible in Oleshky.

Only those who die of natural causes could be buried, she added, and as a result, "some bodies have been on the streets since December".

Bodies are "either getting piled" up in the local hospital morgue, "where there's been no power since winter", says volunteer Ksenia Arkhipova, or "stray dogs eat them".

That detail has been verified by the BBC based on numerous pictures obtained from residents. They are all too graphic to publish.

"This is a tool of psychological pressure," says Ester Vrataryova, the co-founder of charity Humanity, which helps people in Oleshky and the wider Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine.

"If you try to bury a dead body, you'll become the next one," she says.

articles.title: Rio das Ostras busca novas tecnologias para produção rural | G1
articles.standfirst: Visita à Pesagro Campos aproxima o Município de pesquisas e novas tecnologias voltadas à agricultura e à pecuária.
articles.summary: Visita à Pesagro Campos aproxima o Município de pesquisas e novas tecnologias voltadas à agricultura e à pecuária.
articles.body:
A visita foi acompanhada pelo engenheiro agrônomo, Benedito Fernandes — Foto: Secom

Técnicos da Secretaria Municipal de Pesca e Agropecuária de Rio das Ostras realizaram uma visita técnica à unidade da Pesagro-Rio, em Campos dos Goytacazes. O objetivo é buscar novas tecnologias, parcerias e soluções que possam contribuir para o fortalecimento da produção rural no Município.

A visita foi acompanhada pelo engenheiro agrônomo, Benedito Fernandes, que apresentou aos técnicos pesquisas e tecnologias desenvolvidas para apoiar agricultores e produtores rurais.

Uma nova variedade de feijão, identificada como UENF 2014, está entre as novidades que deverá ser testada em Rio das Ostras. A iniciativa poderá contribuir para a avaliação do desempenho da cultura nas condições de solo e clima do Município, buscando alternativas para ampliar e fortalecer a produção agrícola local.

De acordo com o superintendente de Gestão Ambiental, Ivan Noé, que responde interinamente pela Secretaria de Pesca e Agropecuária, durante a visita, também foram apresentados resultados de pesquisas que poderão colaborar para o desenvolvimento da pecuária em Rio das Ostras, com novas variedades de forrageiras, que são compostas por capim e vegetações.

“As novas tecnologias têm potencial para melhorar a alimentação dos animais e contribuir para o fortalecimento da atividade no campo. A aproximação entre a Secretaria e instituições de pesquisa representa mais um passo na busca por inovação e desenvolvimento sustentável para a zona rural de Rio das Ostras”, disse o secretário.

A proposta é levar conhecimento e novas tecnologias ao produtor rural, criando oportunidades para melhorar a produção e ampliar o desenvolvimento das atividades agrícolas e pecuárias no Município.

articles.title: Why is Kenya turning against Tata Chemicals in Magadi?
articles.summary: A century-old industry faces a reckoning over regulation, jobs and local benefits.
articles.body:
Magadi, Kenya – For more than a century, soda ash has shaped life in Magadi, a remote town on the shores of Lake Magadi in Kenya’s Kajiado County.

The mineral has brought exports, jobs and business. But for many people living around the lake, that activity has not brought enough opportunities or basic services. The result is a complicated relationship with Tata Chemicals Magadi, the company that has mined soda ash there for generations.

Now that relationship is under strain. The Kenyan government has suspended the company’s mining operations, and President William Ruto has ordered it to leave while a joint technical committee works with the company to resolve outstanding issues.

For Magadi, the dispute is also about what the community and Kenya have gained from a resource extracted there for more than a century.

Commercial soda ash production in Magadi dates back to 1911. Tata Chemicals acquired the operation in 2005 and later renamed it Tata Chemicals Magadi Limited.

The company has become one of Kenya’s major soda ash exporters, with much of its production destined for international markets. It has also become part of everyday life in Magadi, providing jobs and supporting services including water, healthcare and education.

But the government says its long history in the area does not exempt Tata from Kenya’s current mining laws.

Mining Cabinet Secretary Hassan Joho told Al Jazeera on September 11 that the regulatory environment changed after the 2010 Constitution and the Mining Act. He said a government-wide compliance audit found that Tata had not applied for a mineral right under the Mining Act and had instead relied on its land concessions.

According to Joho, Tata made its first application for a mineral right on July 26, 2024, after which the government began engaging with the company over compliance.

“Past oversights do not grant immunity from existing laws,” Joho said.

He said the review also identified issues around mineral royalties, community development agreements, local processing, employment of Kenyan citizens, procurement of local goods and services, and outstanding matters with the Kajiado County government.

The government says Kenya should get more value from the resource instead of mainly exporting it as a raw material.

Ruto has made a similar argument, saying communities have not benefitted enough from the mineral extracted from Magadi. During his visit to Kajiado, he said a new investor should establish major glass and chemical manufacturing facilities in the county, creating jobs and keeping more value in Kenya.

The government’s decision has raised a question for a company that has operated in Magadi for more than a century: why now?

Joho told Al Jazeera that the answer lies in the government’s decision to carry out comprehensive compliance audits across the mining sector, including legacy concessions.

The ministry suspended Tata’s operations in July, citing regulatory concerns. Since then, the company and the government have been negotiating over how to resolve the outstanding issues.

Tata disputes the suggestion that it has ignored regulatory requirements.

In a statement to Al Jazeera, the company said its subsidiary submitted a comprehensive response to the ministry on August 11 regarding the issues raised in the July 28 suspension notice. Tata said the submission included information on its compliance with applicable regulations and that it was waiting for further direction from the ministry.

The company said it respected the authority of the Kenyan government and remained committed to constructive engagement with concerned agencies and regulators.

The economic stakes are significant. The Standard has previously reported that Tata’s Magadi operation contributes substantially to Kenya’s economy and that the company has argued that a shutdown would affect exports, foreign exchange and employment.

The operation supports hundreds of workers directly, while thousands more people in Magadi depend on the wider economy around it.

A community caught between dependence and frustration

For residents, the debate is not simply about whether Tata should stay or go. It is about what they have received from a company that has been at the centre of Magadi’s economy for generations, and what they could lose if it leaves.

Nkanoi Matipei, a Magadi resident, said locals want more jobs at different levels, more corporate social responsibility projects and access to land under Tata that they say is currently idle and used for grazing.

Another resident, Esther Nganoni, strongly opposed the idea of removing Tata.

“Tata Chemicals Company has been our lifeline,” Nganoni told Al Jazeera, pointing to bursaries, water and health services provided by the company.

She questioned what a replacement investor would offer the community and said residents must be consulted before any decision is made.

Cosmas Karera Kiratu, who previously served as the subcounty children officer for Kajiado West, told Al Jazeera that Magadi faces serious challenges, including poverty, water shortages, long distances to schools, inadequate infrastructure and teachers, child labour, teenage pregnancy, female genital mutilation and child marriage.

He said some schools are about 15km (9 miles) apart, while water remains particularly difficult to access.

According to Karera, the only clean water available through a piped system is supplied to Tata Chemicals from Ngurumani, about 40km (25 miles) away.

Residents depend heavily on Tata water bowsers, which he said do not reach all communities and often provide insufficient water for both domestic and livestock use.

“The local community was very dependent on Tata company in terms of water, health services, school bursary and schools upgrading,” Karera said.

He warned that an abrupt end to Tata’s operations could have serious consequences if alternative services are not put in place.

The technical committee and what happens next

That uncertainty is now at the centre of the government’s negotiations with Tata.

Joho said the ministry’s suspension was intended to give the company an opportunity to address the identified compliance issues. After Tata committed to remedy the outstanding matters, he said, a joint technical committee was established to guide the process.

Joho said the committee is dealing with the formation and gazettement of Community Development Agreement Committees, local processing facilities, outstanding mineral royalties, employment of Kenyan citizens, procurement of local goods and services and unresolved matters with the Kajiado County government.

“Deliberations within the joint technical committee remain progressive, with a clear focus on achieving full statutory compliance under the Mining Act and securing socioeconomic returns for the extractive sector, the local community, and the nation at large,” Joho told Al Jazeera.

The Standard reported that the committee is also considering mineral beneficiation and in-country value addition, outstanding community benefits and royalties, unresolved land matters, the possibility of opening the area to multiple mineral extraction companies and outstanding issues involving Kajiado County.

For Kajiado Governor Joseph Ole Lenku, the county government must have a seat at the table.

“We want to thank the president for his firm stand and directives on Tata Chemicals Magadi. I have been vindicated,” Lenku told Al Jazeera.

He said county participation in negotiations was non-negotiable and identified payment of accrued land rates as the county government’s “irreducible minimum”.

He also said the grievances of Magadi residents had been known and repeated for years.

The government has made clear that if a new investor eventually comes in, it wants more than the export of soda ash. It wants processing, manufacturing, jobs and a larger share of the economic value to remain in Kenya.

But residents are asking what happens to the services and livelihoods that currently depend on Tata.

For Matipei, keeping Tata does not mean accepting the status quo. She wants more jobs, greater community investment and access to land that residents say remains underused.

For Nganoni, removing Tata without a clear alternative could put the community at risk. She argues that residents must be involved in deciding what comes next.

Lenku wants the county government’s interests addressed, while Joho says the government’s objective is to bring the operation fully within Kenya’s mining laws and ensure that the country and local community receive greater socioeconomic benefits.

Tata says it is waiting for the government’s response to its August submission and remains committed to resolving the outstanding issues through engagement.

For Matipei, however, the question is what the community has gained from an industry that has shaped Magadi for generations.

“Over the years, the company’s assistance to the local community has been trickling, sustaining us but denying us economic freedom,” Matipei told Al Jazeera.

The plant has provided jobs and essential services for generations, but residents and officials are pressing for greater local benefits from the resource [Hafsa Sheikh/Al Jazeera]
The plant’s future is now under scrutiny as the government pushes for greater regulatory compliance and wants more value from the resource to remain in Kenya [Hafsa Sheikh/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: Eight US sailors in USS Abraham Lincoln strike group attempted suicide, Navy says
articles.summary: In a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the crew had adequate mental health support during the long deployment.
articles.body:
Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao has said that eight crew members who were assigned to the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide during their lengthy deployment.

The disclosure was made in a letter to Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York on Tuesday in response to questions from the Democrat on the well-being of sailors onboard following mounting concerns.

Family members of sailors had raised alarm about deteriorating mental health and grim conditions during a prolonged mission in the Middle East as part of the US war in Iran.

The carrier, which had been deployed since last November, is now returning to the US. The BBC has contacted the US Navy for comment.

In his letter, Cao said that there were five chaplains and multiple mental health professionals available on board to meet the "spiritual and emotional needs of the crew".

He said the eight sailors included "the Lincoln crew and sailors from the carrier airwing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff, escorting destroyers and all embarked aviation squadrons".

While the US Navy has previously acknowledged supply challenges on the carrier, it denied that a mental health crisis was taking place on the Lincoln, which had some 5,000 crew aboard.

Cao's letter also denied widespread concerns about broken plumbing and shortages of fresh food, but acknowledged temporary "localized piping failures" and problems with the reverse osmosis desalination units, and some meal options were reduced for a "short time".

Senator Gillibrand, a member of the Senate's armed services committee, criticised the Trump administration's previous responses to reports of grim conditions, calling the treatment of service members "completely unacceptable".

"What Trump and Secretary Hegseth dismissed as 'fake news' turned out to be serious and deteriorating conditions for our service members," she said in a statement to the BBC on Wednesday.

"Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect," she added.

The carrier left California in November for the South China Sea and was sent to the Middle East ahead of attacks on Iran in February. The deployment, which was originally set to end in May, was repeatedly extended.

In August, the USS George Washington, an aircraft carrier, was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln following a nine-month deployment.

US sailors stopped in Thailand on their way home, hitting bars, malls and beach areas in their first time on land before continuing on to the US.

Suicide remains a leading cause of death in the US Navy and Marines, according to an analysis of military data by USNI News, while veterans have higher rates of suicide than Americans who have not served in the military, according to the Veterans Administration.

A study of 956 sailors released in January 2025 found that troops aboard US Navy ships suffer the highest rates of "serious psychological distress" compared to other branches of the US military.

The study cited "unique stressors, such as poor habitability, noise and demanding schedules that leave inadequate time for sleep and rest".

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line or you can call the US Suicide and Crisis Lifeline on 988.

articles.title: Tylenol murders mystery deepens after sheriff’s office solves decades-old ‘Unknown Wanderer’ cold case
articles.summary: A man who died in 1982 of cyanide poisoning in an Idaho church has been identified, raising questions about the Chicago Tylenol murders.
articles.body: A mysterious man who died of cyanide poisoning inside an Idaho church more than four decades ago has finally been identified, and investigators say his past raises questions about a possible connection to the still-unsolved 1982 Chicago Tylenol murders. The man known for decades as the "Unknown Wanderer" was Dr. Mathew Francis Betkouski, an organic chemist with a history of discussing cyanide and poison, the Ada County Sheriff's Office in Boise announced Wednesday. Investigators said they couldn't place Betkouski in Chicago during the final week of September 1982, when seven people died after taking Tylenol capsules laced with cyanide, and they are not naming him as a suspect. TYLENOL MURDERS SUSPECT GAVE EERIE FINAL INTERVIEW BEFORE DEATH Dr. Park Dietz, a forensic psychiatrist who was consulted during the original Tylenol investigation and reviewed the evidence gathered on Betkouski, offered a stronger assessment. "It's an extraordinary thing to have been around at the beginning in 1982, and now today in 2026, to see very likely closure," Dietz said. Dietz said groups of forensic psychiatrists, psychologists and criminal profilers who were anonymously presented with information about Betkouski overwhelmingly considered him a viable suspect. Betkouski died on Dec. 4, 1982, after walking into Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise. Authorities determined he died from cyanide poisoning, but he carried no identification, and his fingerprints produced no match. REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY The mystery endured for decades until investigators traced one of nearly 30 keys found on him to Jacksonville, Florida, where Betkouski had lived. DNA recovered from his wallet and later compared with a sample from his brother helped establish his identity. Investigators subsequently uncovered several details that drew their attention to the Tylenol case. A former colleague recalled Betkouski discussing the "perfect crime" and cyanide, while another scientist recalled him saying poison could be introduced into over-the-counter capsules, according to investigators. Authorities also found a map of Chicago and a bottle of sodium cyanide among belongings kept at his family's Los Angeles home. Investigators stressed that the poison was not the potassium cyanide used in the Tylenol murders. THE TYLENOL MURDERS: A LOOK BACK AT THE RASH OF 1982 DRUG STORE POISONINGS Photos showed Betkouski had visited Chicago, but investigators determined they were likely taken in December 1981 and said they cannot establish that he returned when the Tylenol poisonings occurred. Betkouski disappeared from his New Mexico home on Oct. 15, 1982, and turned up dead in Boise seven weeks later after apparently changing his appearance. articles.title: Trump likely ‘smirked’ as 'crass' Iranian president lashed out at US in UN speech: expert
articles.summary: Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. and Israel of attacking Iran at the United Nations, and an expert says Trump likely responded with a smirk.
articles.body: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s sharp rebuke of Washington at the United Nations would have drawn little more than a "smirk" from President Donald Trump, who knows he "holds the cards," a foreign policy expert told Fox News Digital Wednesday. The assessment came after Pezeshkian and Trump addressed the U.N. General Assembly in New York from the same podium within 24 hours of one another, trading sharp rhetoric as tensions between Washington and Tehran continue to mount. "Trump understands he holds the cards, and he may not even have paid much attention to what the Iranian president was saying," Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Fox News Digital. Pezeshkian accused the United States and Israel of attacking Iran while portraying his country as the victim of aggression. THE TOP MOMENTS FROM IRAN PRESIDENT’S TENSE VISIT TO US SOIL AS WAR RAGES "We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists," Pezeshkian claimed. "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country. America and Israel attacked us." "I’m sure that would have drawn a smirk or a smile or a chuckle from the president’s face, seeing that crassness," Taleblu said, pointing to what he described as a sharp contrast between Pezeshkian’s rhetoric and the Iranian government’s track record. Pezeshkian’s address came after Trump used the same U.N. stage to defend the U.S. conflict with Iran and warn that Tehran faces a stark choice between reaching a deal and facing further destruction. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?" Trump said on Tuesday. While the rhetoric from both leaders was pointed, Taleblu said their broader diplomatic positions remain largely predictable. TRUMP TO ZERO-IN ON IRAN NUCLEAR THREAT, GAZA PLAN AND UN OVERHAUL IN WORLD STAGE SPEECH "To a certain degree, both President Trump and President Pezeshkian’s speeches before the U.N. General Assembly’s 81st session were predictable," Taleblu said. "Predictable because the status of both countries and their foreign policy toward the other are in a fairly predictable pattern right now." Despite the threats and recriminations, the two adversaries also appear to be still testing a diplomatic path behind the scenes. Trump said Tuesday that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner spoke with Iranian officials for roughly three hours on the sidelines of the General Assembly and characterized the discussions as productive. Witkoff later said the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the U.S. and Iranian delegations. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also represented Tehran in the discussions, according to reports. KUSHNER TOUTS UNPRECEDENTED IRAN CONTACTS AS TEHRAN DENIES TRUMP BACKCHANNEL Both sides, Taleblu said, are attempting "to make time a weapon on their side" and "to put the burden of choosing between escalation and engagement on the other." But Taleblu went on to characterize Pezeshkian’s broader message as an attempt to cast Iran as a victim through an anti-American, anti-Israel and anti-imperialist framework. "It seemed to be more of a global South, anti-American, anti-Israeli, kind of anti-colonial, anti-imperialist message that he was looking to kind of paint the Islamic Republic as the victim," Taleblu said. "In reality, the long-serving victim in this entire crisis is the Iranian people because of the policies of the Islamic Republic." The competing messages — confrontation from the U.N. podium and diplomacy behind the scenes — highlighted the unresolved tensions between Washington and Tehran as officials explore whether negotiations can produce an off-ramp from the conflict. TRUMP KEEPS FORECASTING AN IRAN DEAL — WHY THE WHITE HOUSE STILL THINKS IT CAN HAPPEN "Despite the tough talk at the podium, both sides still feel like they need to signal an interest in talks, even though they’re both trying to use talks to shape an outcome that is more conducive to their interests," Taleblu said. Pezeshkian also told the General Assembly that Tehran would not surrender to military pressure while signaling that Iran remained open to diplomacy. "I think the Iranians are trying to signal an interest in talks, but they may run into a brick wall quite soon if they foot-drag or delay or don’t meaningfully provide any kind of substantive change in their policy," Taleblu said, citing Iran’s positions on the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz and its nuclear program. "Ultimately, if the positions remain the same, the fact that they’re oscillating between shooting and talking doesn’t mean much because the red lines haven’t actually moved. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Of course, the Trump administration is looking for a political win here."

articles.title: In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
articles.summary: With four measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania, health officials are hoping to get people on board with vaccines in private.
articles.body:
For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.

As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.

Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.

"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.

"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."

The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.

The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.

But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.

The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-skeptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.

Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US.

"They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."

Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.

About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.

There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.

"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.

Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.

"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."

He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.

Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.

Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.

Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings.

"People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"

The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.

In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.

Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it.

"You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.

People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.

But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children.

"There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."

The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.

After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.

Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.

Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable.

"I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.

Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe.

"What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."

The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread.

"I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

articles.title: Venezuela’s acting leader, at U.N. for first address, promises elections at the ‘right moment’
articles.summary: Delcy Rodríguez took over in Venezuela after a surprise U.S. military raid in January that captured then-leader Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges.
articles.body: Venezuela’s acting president, delivering her first address to the U.N. General Assembly since coming to power, promised elections Wednesday and said the nation’s people will determine the “right moment.” “I wish to state this very clearly before this General Assembly: Elections will be held in Venezuela,” Delcy Rodríguez said, adding that her government has started a “political dialogue with opposition sectors” to secure a “process based on equal conditions for all.” Rodríguez said the Venezuelan people will determine the best time to get elections moving and assured the United Nations that, when the time comes, the country’s institutions “will be prepared to guarantee an inclusive and transparent process.” Rodríguez took over in Venezuela after a surprise U.S. military raid in January that captured then-leader Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges. This is the first trip to the United States by a Venezuelan head of state since 2018, when Maduro traveled to New York to participate in the U.N. General Assembly himself. He is being held only a few miles from the organization’s headquarters as he awaits trial. Rodríguez’s participation in the international forum also marks a milestone in Venezuela’s reintegration into global diplomacy. She faced a delicate balance in her closely watched U.N. speech, which needed to be addressed to both her people and the U.S. government that holds her predecessor. She said her country is coming back strong after “setbacks” suffered this year and thanked President Donald Trump for being willing to resume relations after the U.S. military spirited her predecessor out of the country. “Today, Venezuela is being reborn,” Rodríguez said in her remarks to the international forum. “I do not promise you an easy way forward,” Rodríguez said, saying she was addressing her people. “Rebuilding our national soul will be the priority.”

articles.title: ‘Home Improvement’ star Jonathan Taylor Thomas detained during traffic stop
articles.summary: Jonathan Taylor Thomas, best known for playing Randy Taylor on “Home Improvement,” was arrested Monday during a traffic stop, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said.
articles.body: Jonathan Taylor Thomas, best known for playing Randy Taylor on “Home Improvement,” was arrested Monday during a traffic stop, the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department said. The 45-year-old actor, whose given name is Jonathan Taylor Weiss, was detained after the car he was riding in was pulled over for a DUI investigation in the Los Angeles area, according to the sheriff’s department. Deputies saw a vehicle that was stopped at an intersection at a green light and was blocking traffic, officials said. They pulled alongside the vehicle to see if the driver needed assistance and noticed the driver was acting oddly and appeared to be intoxicated, the sheriff’s department said. Deputies then stopped the vehicle and conducted a driving under the influence investigation. Thomas was a passenger and appeared intoxicated, the department said. While sobriety tests were being performed on the driver, Thomas “continually exited the vehicle and approached the deputies, distracting them from their investigation,” the sheriff’s department said. “Deputies attempted to detain (Thomas) for obstruction and public intoxication, at which point, (Thomas) kicked a deputy in the stomach,” the sheriff’s department said. The actor was arrested and taken to a sheriff’s station where he was booked, officials told NBC News. The driver was also arrested and booked for driving under the influence of alcohol, according to the sheriff’s department. According to jail records, Thomas was arrested at 1:50 a.m. Monday and released at 12 p.m. Tuesday. Reps for Thomas did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The sheriff’s department said Thomas’ case will be presented to county prosecutors for consideration of criminal charges. Thomas has kept out of the public eye for years, with his last acting credit being a 2015 appearance on Tim Allen’s show “Last Man Standing,” according to IMDb. He also directed a 2016 episode of the series. In July, his “Home Improvement” on-screen mom, Patricia Richardson, posted a photo with him and cast member Taran Noah Smith on Instagram. Thomas, a ’90s heartthrob, is also known for his roles in “Man of the House,” “Tom and Huck,” “Wild America” and “8 Simple Rules,” among others. He also voiced young Simba in “The Lion King.”

articles.title: They were labelled 'pervert glasses'. Will a camera-free version transform their image?
articles.summary: Meta has unveiled audio-only smart glasses, with some questioning whether it is a response to the backlash over privacy.
articles.body:
When Meta first launched its AI-powered smart glasses in 2023, in collaboration with the trendy sunglasses brand Ray-Ban, it unleashed a storm of controversy.

There have been multiple reports of the devices being used to harass women and girls in particular , filming them without their consent, then sharing the footage.

The image problem doesn't seem to have been cured by Meta's enlistment this summer of Kylie Jenner, Kim Kardashian's sister, as their prime model. The devices have been dubbed "pervert" or "creepy" glasses. In the UK, JD Wetherspoon pubs, a handful of major theatres, Comic-Con, some schools, and Faslane, home of the UK's nuclear submarines, have all chosen to ban them.

On Thursday, Meta is unveiling a new version which does not contain a camera at all, called Ray-Ban Meta Audio. They will have the audio functions of the original glasses - including the ability to make phone calls or play music, with the sound funnelled directly into your ear - but with fewer implications for privacy.

To some in the industry, it looks like an interesting pivot - a response, perhaps, to the backlash over privacy.

The tech giant denies that the new glasses have been rushed out in response to public anger. They say the product has been in development for two years. The audio-only version is cheaper than its camera-enabled cousins, and Meta says it has a lighter frame and better battery life.

When I put it to Meta Glasses' head of product Ankit Brahmbhatt that I thought they might overtake the original camera-enabled glasses in sales, there was a pregnant pause.

"We have, I think, something for everyone," he said, choosing his words very carefully.

Does the release of a camera-free option represent a shift in how tech companies see the future of smart glasses? And is Meta's original vision getting further away?

Or should we see camera-free glasses as a niche side-product that serves a small market - a bit like how some mobile manufacturers are now releasing internet-disabled "brick" phones for people who are tired of social media?

There's no doubt that smart glasses have become controversial.

I was lent a pair of Meta Ray-Bans – with cameras - to try out. I was initially nervous about wearing them in public, in case someone got physical: I have heard of people knocking them off wearers' heads and smashing them in the street.

The reality was that I wore them on public transport and on foot in several cities including London, Glasgow and Portsmouth, and nobody batted an eyelid. It made me wonder whether awareness of them is really as high as both Meta and anti-glasses campaigners believe.

That said, some people quietly told me they would not be confident enough to approach someone wearing them even if they did spot them, for fear of the interaction being filmed and uploaded.

The glasses are designed to work as an extension of your phone. They use Bluetooth to sync with a handset via Meta's AI app. They are voice-activated, with open speakers in the arms funnelling sound into your ears. The result is a bit like wearing headphones without the addition of noise-cancelling features, so you can still hear the world around you.

My potentially cancellable opinion is that I found many of the glasses' features useful. Interestingly, none of them included the camera.

Listening to music and podcasts on the move without having earbuds stuffed into my ears felt safer. I felt more confident about avoiding the gamut of e-bike-riding phone thieves in central London without my phone physically in my hand.

And as someone with a pitiful sense of direction, I rely a lot on map apps. It was handy to have the directions spoken in my ears. The pay-off for this, however, was having to accept allowing the Meta AI app to know exactly where I was at all times. Meta is notorious for its hunger for personal data.

When I posted about using the Meta Ray-Bans on social media, I got a bit of a hard time. Less so when I showed them to people in my everyday life.

My hairdresser loved the idea of using them to record her clients' hair transformations. A builder I chatted to at the gym reckoned they would be useful on sites for recording what he was doing, either in the event of an accident or even to teach others new skills. My friend who runs said he would like to wear them on a jog.

Plenty of content creators are big fans. My son borrowed them to wash my car, and was proud of his film showing me how he delicately chipped away at a stubborn bit of bird poo without damaging the paintwork (I was pleased, and happy to take his word for it).

More broadly, smart glasses have been welcomed by the blind community. One user described them to the BBC as a "game-changer" because they can give audio descriptions of current locations and read out visible text like restaurant menu options. Earlier this year Meta donated 15,000 pairs to a charity for the blind in Ireland.

But still, anger over privacy has grown.

The glasses have a blinking white LED that switches on when the camera is active, but a whole industry has sprung up around finding technical workarounds to disable that light, some of which involve taking the glasses apart.

Meta says less than 0.1% of the frames it has sold worldwide have been physically tampered with. Exact sales figures are unknown, but Ray-Ban's parent company EssilorLuxottica has reported that it sold seven million last year.

Liz Hunter, a tech founder and parent who has set up a petition calling for urgent new regulation of smart glasses, is furious.

"They should never, ever have left the lab at Meta," she told me. "It's a real travesty of public trust, and of women's equality, and it's rolled back our privacy rights right before our very eyes."

Hunter thinks smart glasses should remain available for blind people, but not for the general population.

"We don't need them, we don't want them," she says.

A Polish developer has released an app called ZuckOff which uses Bluetooth to identify nearby smart glasses. It's been downloaded thousands of times, reports Wired magazine.

Ben Wood, from tech research firm CCS Insight, remembers first reading the phrase "pervert glasses" in the usually strait-laced Financial Times - a sign, he says, that it had prompted a "significant public backlash".

The furore has not deterred other companies from eyeing the market, however.

Samsung is reported to be working on a collaboration with the upmarket glasses brand Warby Parker. Google is also said to be working on a set. Snap, the firm behind Snapchat, has just launched Specs, which are retailing in the US for $2,195 (and £1,995 in the UK). Users can see data inside the glass, and snap their fingers to take a photo.

Snap founder Evan Spiegel says he thinks smart glasses will eventually replace phones, and he's not alone.

When Meta launched smart glasses in 2021, they were geared in part around what the user could see. The firm promised they would allow users to "easily record the world as you see it", and to "capture life's moments as they happen from a unique first-person perspective".

So Meta's latest announcement - glasses without a camera - is notable.

Janusz Swierczynski, a researcher at Oxford University's Saïd Business School, who is worried about smart glasses, says the release of a camera-free version is a "positive sign" that Meta seems to have listened to privacy concerns. "They're thinking about it and that they're responding," he says, though he thinks it's "not a perfect" response because the camera-enabled glasses are still on the market.

Others are less sure it represents a real shift.

"It's certainly not the end of cameras in glasses," says Wood, from CCS Insight. He thinks that smart glasses are largely about capturing information; the glasses collect as much data as they can from your surroundings and then use AI to tell you about it.

And glasses armed with a camera - trained on whatever you can see - are an "extremely good" source of that information.

"That is an invaluable data stream to an AI platform, which can then interpret that data and provide you with the best possible information related to it," Wood says. "So having the vision parts of it with the cameras is a key pillar for getting the best experience."

How the social media ban could reshape how all of us use the internet

AI 'slop' is transforming social media - and a backlash is brewing

Tech billionaires seem to be doom prepping. Should we all be worried?

He imagines Meta has been working on the camera-free glasses for several years, and the current backlash over privacy provides "fantastic timing" for their release.

Indeed, Meta doesn't yet show any signs of slowing down its development of camera-enabled glasses. The company is bringing its third generation of the glasses to the UK next month. These can visually display data inside the specs' lenses. (As a live broadcast journalist who has talked openly about brain fog, I can see the appeal of glasses that can discreetly display a script).

Kate Winick, a tech analyst at the research firm Forrester, says it's not a step back from camera-enabled glasses but more of a "half step to the side, where they give users time to get comfortable with the technology… so that users themselves start to say, 'Oh, this would be so much more useful if it had a camera'."

And she says, paradoxically, the existence of camera-free glasses might help "take the heat" off people who wear camera-enabled glasses in public. "It's now clear that out in the market some glasses have cameras and some don't," she says. "You can't automatically get mad at everybody wearing Meta's glasses, because you may not know whether or not they have a camera."

And other companies are trying to address privacy concerns in different ways - without getting rid of the camera.

The Taiwanese firm HTC recently launched Vive Eagle glasses, which cost less than a quarter of Snap's.

Thomas Dexmier, a vice president at HTC Vive, says that if anyone near an Eagle specs wearer says "stop filming" or "stop recording", and it is picked up by one of the four microphones, the camera will deactivate.

And he adds that all recordings captured by the glasses are encrypted, and the firm itself cannot see them - though this also means HTC cannot flag harmful content.

"We acknowledge that there are some challenges, potentially becoming a real problem, especially for women," he said.

He said HTC Vive was working to make it as difficult as possible for the tech to be misused but said it was "too early to comment" on whether the firm would consider a version without cameras.

Ultimately, Wood thinks that camera-enabled glasses are "not going away".

He says the current moment reminds him of the 2000s, when some people said that mobile phone companies couldn't install cameras in their devices because of similar concerns over privacy. "There's an inevitability there," he says.

"We will have to find a societal norm, a framework for the use of these products."

articles.title: In 2025, an British charity shop priced a Chinese plate at £2; expert identified it as Imperial porcelain, and it sold for £7,620
articles.summary: A Chinese porcelain dish bought for £2 at a charity shop in Blandford Forum has sold for £7,620 after an expert identified its connection to the Chinese
articles.body: A Chinese porcelain dish bought for £2 at a charity shop in Blandford Forum has sold for £7,620 after an expert identified its connection to the Chinese Imperial Collection. The blue and yellow "five dragon" dish was examined by John Axford, chairman of Woolley and Wallis and an Asian art specialist, who recognised its period from its distinctive decoration. A six-character Emperor Daoguang mark, dating to 1821–1850, further confirmed its link to the Chinese Imperial Collection. The dish was given an auction estimate of £1,500 to £2,000 before being sold at Woolley and Wallis. The proceeds went directly to the charity.The £2 Chinese plate was identified as Imperial porcelainFurther examination of the dish revealed a six-character Emperor Daoguang mark. According to the BBC, this mark, associated with the period from 1821 to 1850, confirmed the dish's link to the Chinese Imperial Collection. The piece was therefore identified as a Chinese imperial porcelain item from the 19th Century.The dish had initially been set to be sold for only £2 at the charity shop, but its identification changed its destination from a charity-shop sale to an auction at Woolley and Wallis. The auction house gave the blue and yellow porcelain dish an estimate of £1,500 to £2,000 before it eventually sold for £7,620.Rare Chinese imperial porcelain rarely appears on the marketAxford told the BBC that pieces of this type do not come onto the market very often. He said such objects are "usually held in public collections or sometimes in private collections", while describing this particular dish as having been left somewhere in the south-west of England before it was discovered at the charity shop.Axford explained that a significant amount of Chinese imperial porcelain was brought back to Europe after the fall of the Qing dynasty. He said that much of the interest in the sale came from mainland China and Hong Kong.Charity benefited directly from the £7,620 Chinese porcelain saleThe £7,620 auction sale was not the only significant detail surrounding the discovery. The proceeds from the dish would go directly to the charity that operated the shop where the porcelain was found.The dish was one of two Chinese porcelain pieces found in British charity shops and later sold at auction. articles.title: 8 Navy members attempted suicide on the USS Lincoln during extended deployment, military official says
articles.summary: The ship, which supported the U.S. war with Iran, was at sea for nearly 300 days without a port call.
articles.body: Eight Navy members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln have attempted suicide since the beginning of their extended deployment, a top Navy official said in a letter obtained by NBC News. The length of the deployment, which some service members on board the carrier had described as extraordinarily tough, has raised concerns about supply shortages and the effect on sailors’ mental health. No deaths have been attributed to suicide during the deployment. The number of suicide attempts includes those by crewmembers and sailors from the carrier air wing, strike group and destroyer squadron staff; escorting destroyers; and all embarked aviation squadrons, according to the letter, which acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao sent to Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y. About 7,500 service members, primarily sailors, are part of the strike group. A Navy official said the letter was delivered to Gillibrand on Tuesday. The official said the number of sailors who jumped overboard while the Lincoln was in the Middle East providing operations for the war in Iran remains at two, as previously reported. The official did not provide details about the six other attempts. In the letter, Cao answered a series of questions that Gillibrand, a member of the Armed Services Committee, had asked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a previous letter. The letter also addressed Gillibrand’s concerns about conditions and medical resources aboard the Lincoln. In a statement, Gillibrand said the conditions on the ship were “serious and deteriorating.” “Our troops and their families make immense sacrifices every single day, yet the president dismissed them with open disrespect,” she said. President Donald Trump has previously said the deployment was “not nearly long enough.” The ship was at sea without a port call for 286 days supporting the U.S. war with Iran. A typical deployment is six to seven months, with regular stops to replenish food supplies. The Lincoln left San Diego in November. Its deployment was supposed to end in May, but it was extended after the war began in February. The ship stopped in Thailand this month and is now sailing back to San Diego after a stop in Guam. Relatives of those on board raised concerns about food shortages and low morale and how the extended time at sea was “wreaking havoc” on sailors’ mental health, as one relative described it to NBC News last month. Some military officials have played down or rejected those claims. In an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal last month, Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, described the concerns as “old news” that were resolved months ago. This summer, a Navy official said that officials had not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship and that service members’ well-being was a top priority. “We take every service member’s well-being seriously and have religious, medical and mental health professionals available to assess and address concerns as they arise,” the official said in a statement. The Lincoln has five chaplains, a clinical psychologist, a clinical social worker, behavioral health technicians and an embedded integrated prevention coordination counselor to support the crew, the Navy official said. If you or someone you know is struggling or in emotional distress, call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org 24/7 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. For additional resources, visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

articles.title: Turkiye agrees to gradual handover of Bashiqa base to Iraq
articles.summary: Iraqi Prime Minister al-Zaidi and Turkish President Erdogan pledged deeper security cooperation at UNGA.
articles.body:
Turkiye and Iraq have agreed to a gradual transfer of Ankara’s military base in northern Iraq’s Bashiqa to Baghdad, according to a statement released by the Iraqi prime minister’s office.

The announcement followed a meeting on Wednesday between Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

“Within this framework, they reached an agreement on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of outlawed foreign armed elements,” Iraq’s prime minister’s office announced, in an apparent reference to the Kurdistan Workers’ Party ( PKK ), which has maintained a presence in the mountainous Sinjar region of northern Iraq.

“The two sides also agreed to expand the volume of bilateral trade and investment, to implement signed agreements immediately, and to accelerate joint strategic projects, particularly the Development Road project,” the office added.

The decision to transfer the facility addresses a longstanding flashpoint between the two neighbours .

Turkiye first established the base in Bashiqa, northeast of Mosul, in December 2015 through an agreement with the autonomous Kurdistan Regional Government to train local forces fighting the ISIL (ISIS) group.

The deployment of up to 600 Turkish soldiers drew criticism from Baghdad, which viewed the presence as a violation of Iraqi sovereignty.

The Sinjar region has long been a focal point for Turkish military operations targeting fighters from the PKK.

Cross-border operations in Sinjar had eased following a landmark peace process between Ankara and the PKK in 2025 , paving the way for federal authorities to assert control over the border zone.

Wednesday’s accord caps months of efforts by Baghdad to consolidate state authority over northern flashpoints, while aligning with Ankara on trade corridors and security coordination along their shared frontier.

articles.title: In 2017, a few volunteers packed 10 backpacks with food for children; nine years later, the programme is feeding thousands of students across Metro Atlanta
articles.summary: Backpack Buddies of Metro Atlanta began in 2017 with a small group of volunteers at a single local elementary school, packing nonperishable food for
articles.body: Backpack Buddies of Metro Atlanta began in 2017 with a small group of volunteers at a single local elementary school, packing nonperishable food for children who faced food insecurity over the weekend. The first distribution served just 10 students. Nine years later, the organisation provides weekend meals to thousands of children across dozens of schools throughout metro Atlanta. Here's how a small volunteer effort grew into a regional programme, and what it takes to keep it running today. It was founded by Ronald and Samra Robbins.How Backpack Buddies started with 10 backpacksThe programme's story began at one local elementary school, where volunteers gathered each week to pack nonperishable food for children facing weekend food insecurity. According to the Backpack Buddies of Metro Atlanta, the bags were discreetly delivered to the school so students could take food home in their backpacks without drawing attention to their circumstances. The idea behind it was simple, if children couldn't rely on school meals over the weekend, the community could help make sure food was available at home. That first distribution reached just 10 students, laying the groundwork for what would grow far beyond a single school.From one school to dozens: How the programme scaled upBackpack Buddies became a registered 501(c)(3) nonprofit in 2022, and during the 2022–2023 school year, it was feeding approximately 800 children across 27 schools. By the start of the 2025–2026 school year, that number had grown to 2,625 children across 53 schools, supported by hundreds of volunteers and 34 Community Buddy organisations. In April 2025, the organisation reached another milestone, delivering its one millionth meal, a figure representing years of food sourcing, inventory management, packing, transportation and school partnerships working together behind the scenes.What goes into a weekend meal, and how the model worksBackpack Buddies provides shelf-stable, kid-friendly food designed specifically for children to have access to meals and snacks over the weekend, including proteins and mains, vegetables, breakfast items, fruits, snacks and drinks. The goal isn't simply to put food into a backpack, but to give children reliable access to food during the days when school meals aren't available. The model relies heavily on Community Buddies, organisations such as religious groups, civic organisations and senior centres that adopt one or more schools and help pack and deliver meals to children identified as needing weekend food assistance.The role of volunteers and what comes nextVolunteers remain central to the programme's operations, helping inventory food, prepare orders, load deliveries and support community events at the organisation's Dunwoody warehouse. As Backpack Buddies has grown, so does its need for volunteer support, since a larger programme means more food to move, more orders to prepare and more schools to serve. The organisation estimates that $250 can feed one child every weekend of the school year, and continues to rely on donations, volunteers and new Community Buddy partnerships to keep expanding its reach across metro Atlanta, where the need for weekend food support has continued to grow alongside the programme itself.You use AI every day. articles.title: Watch: RAF Hawk T2 crashes and explodes near airbase in Wales
articles.summary: A Royal Air Force Hawk T2 training aircraft crashed near RAF Valley on Anglesey in north Wales on Wednesday after both pilots ejected from the jet shortly
articles.body: A Royal Air Force Hawk T2 training aircraft crashed near RAF Valley on Anglesey in north Wales on Wednesday after both pilots ejected from the jet shortly after takeoff. The two pilots were later treated for minor injuries.According to The Guardian, the aircraft had just taken off from RAF Valley when it appeared to develop trouble and crashed near Pencarnisiog, less than two miles from the airbase. Video footage showed the aircraft descending steeply before hitting the ground and exploding.An RAF spokesperson said, “An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley, occurred near Anglesey. An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time.”North Wales Police said, “Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries.” Police officers attended the scene alongside RAF personnel and other emergency services.The fire was brought under control and members of the public were asked to avoid the area while emergency services worked at the site.The RAF later announced that it had temporarily paused Hawk T1 and T2 operations as a precautionary measure while investigations into the crash continue. The Hawk T1 is also used by the Red Arrows, while Hawk T2 aircraft are used for advanced fast jet training.UK defence secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X, “My thoughts are first and foremost with the pilots. We will provide further updates in due course.”The BAE Systems Hawk T2, also known as the Hawk 128, is a two-seat advanced jet trainer operated by the Royal Air Force. It is a transonic, fully aerobatic aircraft designed to prepare pilots for frontline fighters such as the Eurofighter Typhoon and F-35B.The Hawk has a modern glass cockpit, advanced avionics, datalink and synthetic radar and electronic warfare systems. These allow trainee pilots to practise combat scenarios and air-intercept missions without the aircraft carrying an actual radar system.RAF Valley in Anglesey operates the Hawk T2 through No 4 Flying Training School. The RAF had a fleet of 28 Hawk T2 aircraft at the base, which forms a key part of Britain's fast-jet pilot training pipeline.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zelenskyy, at UN, urges leaders to keep choking Russia's revenues and impede its war efforts
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told world leaders Wednesday that Vladimir Putin is the only obstacle to ending \"the ridiculous and never-ending
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told world leaders Wednesday that Vladimir Putin is the only obstacle to ending "the ridiculous and never-ending war," and he urged nations large and small to pressure the Russian president for peace by choking the country's revenues and impeding its war efforts."Our target is Russia's ability to finance this war, to drag it out, to make it more brutal and more destructive," Zelenskyy told the U.N. General Assembly's annual global gathering. "Russia's finances and Russia's production are what must be stopped if Putin is to be stopped."When Russia gets money from trade, "it always says no to diplomacy," Zelenskyy argued, "so Russia's revenues must remain a target."Earlier Wednesday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov clashed with Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and her country's European supporters at a UN Security Council meeting, and Lavrov and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio met on the assembly sidelines and discussed the war.Top US diplomat talks about potential for a ceasefireRubio later told reporters that Russia and Ukraine have expressed interest in a limited ceasefire that would halt attacks on grain shipments - both countries are major exporters -- and on each country's energy sectors, which have been targeted in escalating drone and missile attacks.Rubio said reaching even a partial deal would be difficult but worthwhile, noting that Zelenskyy has publicly endorsed such a plan. The United States would be willing to help make it happen, Rubio said.Russia's Foreign Ministry made no mention of a partial deal on grain shipments in a statement after the Lavrov-Rubio meeting. The statement reiterated that the root causes of what it calls its "special military operation" must be addressed.At the Security Council, Lavrov said Russia will not "pause" its military action, claiming Europe would use it to "pump" Ukraine with weapons. He also made no mention of any kind of grain and energy deal, called Ukraine's government "terrorists," and Moscow's military operation aims to ensure Russia's security and the rights of Russian speakers.Lavrov is due to address the General Assembly on Saturday.Zelenskyy cast doubt on Russia's interest in ending the fighting. "Something always seems to stop Putin from saying, 'That's it. Enough. Peace,'" Zelenskyy said. "Can you even imagine him without war? He is 'patient zero', the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further.""The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else," the Ukrainian president warned.The war has reverberated across the planet -- with global repercussions for fuel, fertilizer and grain shipments - and for geopolitics, widening divisions between Russia and the West.Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, expecting to take the capital, Kyiv, in a week. But Ukraine rallied to defend its sovereignty, and the conflict has dragged on, with front-line positions in eastern and southern Ukraine largely unchanged since last year.Western analysts estimate that over 500,000 Russian troops have been killed and that Ukraine has recorded more than 500,000 military casualties, including up to 140,000 deaths. Neither country discloses its own casualty totals.Russia and Ukraine have intensified their long-range attacks with drones and missiles, and Russian drones pounded Kyiv Wednesday, killing two people and wounding 23; two others were injured by a strike that started a big fire at a shopping mall in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia.Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck Ukrainian military-industrial and energy facilities, logistics centers, and sea vessels overnight. The ministry said its air defenses intercepted more than 500 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions and Crimea, as well as the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. Crimea is the peninsula that Russia seized by force and illegally annexed in 2014.Zelenskyy says 'you can stand and survive'Zelenskyy told the assembly that Russia has used 63,000 attack drones of different types against Ukraine so far this year alone. While celebrating that his own country "has proven that even against a much bigger enemy, you can stand and survive," he implored world leaders to deny Putin money or foreign fighters."Limit his money. Limit his war," the Ukrainian leader said.Zelenskyy said Ukraine must boost its military and has already successfully tested four new jet-powered interceptor drones against Iranian-designed Shahed drones used by Russia in Ukraine. He also heralded drone and anti-ballistic missile agreements and programs with various countries.Zelenskyy worried, however, that artificial intelligence "will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield" with the development of autonomous killer weapons."We need peace before we reach that point," he said."Sometimes, it may seem that Ukraine is focused, focused, only on war because we speak about weapons, we speak about defense and sanctions against the aggressor. But Ukrainians did not choose this war," Zelenskyy said. "We choose not to die. .... We are defending ourselves."You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel moves to bar both main Arab lists from October election
articles.summary: Excluding Ra’am and the Joint List leaves Palestinian citizens in Israel without major Knesset representation options.
articles.body:
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has voted to bar both main Arab electoral lists from next month’s election, putting the political representation of Palestinian citizens of Israel before the Supreme Court weeks before voters go to the polls.

The committee voted on Wednesday to disqualify the United Arab List, or Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, and the Joint List, an alliance of the Arab-led Hadash, Ta’al and Balad parties. It also voted separately to bar Hadash legislator Ofer Cassif and Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh. The election is scheduled for October 27.

The bans are not final. Decisions against individual candidates require Supreme Court approval, while lists can appeal their exclusion. Adalah, the legal centre representing the parties and candidates, says it will challenge the votes when the court hears the cases next week.

Ra’am called its exclusion “political and unacceptable”, saying the decision was intended to prevent it from influencing the balance of power and changing the government.

The Joint List said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir were trying to discourage Arab citizens from voting “because they fear our ability to bring down the government of genocide and racism”. Its leader, Yousef Jabareen, questioned how the committee could bar parties representing more than 1.25 million voters.

Abu Shehadeh told Al Jazeera that his exclusion was an attempt to silence criticism of government policy and said the decisions would be challenged in court and through public protest. Rejecting the allegation that he supports violence, he told The Times of Israel: “I have never called for violence or terrorism. I oppose armed struggle.”

The petitions invoke Section 7A of Basic Law: The Knesset, which allows a list or candidate to be excluded for denying Israel’s existence as a “Jewish and democratic state”, inciting racism or supporting armed struggle against Israel by an enemy state or an organisation designated as terrorist.

Netanyahu’s Likud party sought to disqualify the Joint List and Cassif, and was among the groups that filed against Ra’am. Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit party also sought to bar Abu Shehadeh. Adalah disputes the allegations. It says the case against Ra’am presents no evidence that the party supports armed struggle, while the Joint List petition relies heavily on old material, including bills proposed in previous Knessets.

Abu Shehadeh’s case has drawn a different response. Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara found no legal basis to exclude the other targeted parties and candidates but said an article he published on October 8, 2023, which she said may constitute support for armed struggle, warranted serious examination. The committee voted 31-4 to bar him. Adalah says the article contains no such call.

The push to bar Abu Shehadeh drew support from parties outside Netanyahu’s coalition. According to The Times of Israel , opposition parties voted to disqualify him, as did Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, who chairs the elections committee. The vote broke with decades of precedent in which committee chairs abstained from disqualification votes. Abu Shehadeh’s exclusion still requires approval from the full Supreme Court.

Ra’am joined the coalition government formed by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid in 2021, helping end Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office in 2021, although Abbas had previously discussed cooperation with Netanyahu as well. Now Likud itself has filed petitions against Arab representation, while Ben-Gvir’s party has pursued separate exclusions.

A Channel 12 poll published on Tuesday projected seven seats for the Joint List and five for Ra’am, against 50 for Netanyahu’s current coalition bloc. The 12 projected Arab seats would not automatically back Netanyahu’s opponents, as mainstream opposition parties remain divided over whether to govern with Arab support. But removing both lists would change the possible routes to the 61-seat majority needed to form a government.

The Supreme Court has overturned previous committee bans on Arab lists and candidates, including Balad’s exclusion in 2022. It must now decide whether the evidence meets the legal threshold for barring the two principal lists seeking to represent Palestinian citizens of Israel. The ruling will determine who can appear on the October ballot.
